title: Classical mechanics
subtitle: Predict motion from interactions
prerequisites: Foundations for the four introductory concepts. The extended sequence uses the Mathematical toolkit: derivatives, integrals, vectors, trigonometry and simple differential equations. Each lesson links its local prerequisites.

lessons.title: Position needs a reference
lessons.idea: Position says where you are; velocity says how your position is changing.
body: Choose a zero place, called the origin, and choose which direction is positive. If right is positive, x = −2 m means two metres left of zero. It does not tell you whether the cart is moving left or right.

With constant velocity, each second adds the same signed change to position. Multiply velocity by elapsed time to find displacement, then add the starting position. Starting at −3 m and moving +2 m each second for 4 seconds adds +8 m, so the finish is +5 m.
Changing the origin changes all position numbers by the same amount. It does not change how far the object moves during each second. Position and change in position are different quantities.
lessons.equation: x(t) = x₀ + vt
lessons.terms: x(t): Position at time t (metres (m)). The parentheses say position depends on time; they do not mean x multiplied by t. x₀: Starting position (m). The subscript 0 marks the value at the chosen start. v: Constant velocity (metres per second (m/s)). The sign gives direction along the chosen axis. t: Elapsed time (seconds (s)). The product vt is displacement in metres.

example.title: Crossing the origin
steps: Start at x₀ = −3 m with v = +2 m/s.
After t = 4 s: x = −3 m + (2 m/s)(4 s) = 5 m.
The displacement is +8 m; the final position is +5 m.

visual.title: Separate start, change and finish
visual.caption: A one-dimensional constant-velocity model in a fixed reference frame.

check.prompt: A cart starts at +5 m and moves at −2 m/s for 2 s. Where is it?
explanations: Yes. Final position x = 5 m + (−2 m/s)(2 s) = 1 m. The displacement is −4 m; add it to the starting position.
−4 m is its displacement, not its final position.
The negative velocity reduces the position: subtract 4 m rather than add it.

apply.title: A moving camera
apply.text: A camera starts 8 m from a marker and moves toward it at 0.5 m/s. How long to reach the marker?
apply.answer: Put the marker at x = 0 and choose away from it as positive. Starting position x₀ = 8 m and velocity v = −0.5 m/s. The position rule becomes 0 m = 8 m − (0.5 m/s)t. Covering 8 metres at half a metre each second takes t = 8 m ÷ (0.5 m/s) = 16 s, if velocity stays constant.

lessons.limits: The model assumes constant velocity and a fixed one-dimensional reference frame. Classical velocities are used well below the speed of light.

lessons.title: Separate an interval average from a local rate
lessons.idea: A trip average and a reading right now answer different questions.
body: Average velocity is the signed change from start position to finish position divided by elapsed time. If you go out and return to the start, that change is zero—even though you travelled.

Instantaneous means “at one moment”. Instantaneous velocity is the rate at which position changes right now. The derivative dx/dt gives that rate; on a position–time graph it is the slope at the chosen moment.

Speed leaves out direction. In one dimension, |v| means the nonnegative size of velocity. Average speed instead uses total travelled distance divided by total time. It is not generally the size of average velocity.
lessons.equation: v_avg = Δx/Δt;  v(t) = dx/dt;  speed = |v|
lessons.terms: x, t: Position and time (metres (m), seconds (s)). x is measured from a chosen zero; t measures time. Δx, Δt: Position change and elapsed time (m, s). Δ means final minus initial value; elapsed time is positive. v_avg, v(t): Average and instantaneous velocity (metres per second (m/s)). The subscript avg means average; (t) means the value can depend on time. dx/dt: Derivative of position with time (m/s). The local rate of position change, taught in the mathematical toolkit. |v|: Speed (m/s). The bars remove the sign, giving a nonnegative size.

example.title: A return trip
steps: Move 6 m right in 3 s, then 6 m left in 3 s.
Net displacement is 0 m, so average velocity over 6 s is 0 m/s.
Distance is 12 m, so average speed is 2 m/s.

visual.title: Separate an interval average from a local rate
visual.caption: Distance tracks the path; displacement compares endpoints. The same trip can give different averages.

check.prompt: A cart follows x(t) = (1 m/s²)t². What is instantaneous velocity at 3 s?
explanations: Yes. Differentiate x(t) to get v = (2 m/s²)t.
3 m/s is the average velocity from 0 to 3 s, not the final instantaneous velocity.
9 m is position at 3 s, not velocity.

apply.title: Read a speedometer
apply.text: Why can the current speedometer reading differ from trip distance divided by trip time?
apply.answer: The speedometer estimates the speed now. The trip calculation averages speed over an interval that may include stops and changes.

lessons.limits: A measured instantaneous velocity is estimated over a finite interval and has uncertainty. The mathematical derivative is an idealization.

equationGuide.meaning: For the whole interval, divide position change by time. For one moment, use the position’s time derivative. Remove the direction sign to get speed.

lessons.title: Compare motion from two observers
lessons.idea: Compare two velocities by first measuring them from the same viewpoint.
body: A reference frame is a choice of positions, directions and clocks used to describe motion. If two carts both move right relative to the floor, the slower cart sees the faster one pull ahead at their velocity difference.

Name the object A and the observer B. Measure both velocities in the same frame and subtract B’s velocity from A’s. Use the same positive direction and units. In more than one dimension, subtract each matching component.

This classical rule is a good approximation when speeds are much smaller than light speed. A viewpoint moving at constant velocity changes the reported velocity, but does not by itself change acceleration.
lessons.equation: v_A relative to B = v_A − v_B
lessons.terms: v_A, v_B: Velocities of A and B (m/s). Both use the same axis and time convention; a sign gives direction. v_A relative to B: Velocity of A seen from B (m/s). How quickly A’s position changes compared with B’s.

example.title: Two moving carts
steps: Cart A moves right at 5 m/s; B moves right at 2 m/s.
Relative velocity of A as seen from B is 5−2 = 3 m/s.
As seen from A, B moves at 2−5 = −3 m/s.

visual.title: Compare motion from two observers
visual.caption: Subtract vector velocities; do not automatically add their magnitudes.

check.prompt: A moves at +4 m/s and B at −1 m/s. What is A’s velocity relative to B?
explanations: The negative sign in B’s velocity must also be subtracted.
That is B’s velocity relative to A.

apply.title: A moving walkway
apply.text: You walk forward at 1 m/s relative to a walkway moving forward at 0.6 m/s relative to the floor. What is your floor-frame velocity?
apply.answer: 1.6 m/s forward in the classical model. Add the walkway velocity to the velocity measured relative to it.

lessons.limits: This velocity transformation is not valid near light speed. Accelerating observer frames require additional care when applying Newton’s laws.

practice.prompt: In one laboratory frame, A moves at +7 m/s and B at −2 m/s. The positive axis points right.
practice.reasoning: The relative velocities are negatives of each other. Stating the observer is part of stating the answer.

equationGuide.meaning: The velocity A has relative to B equals A’s velocity minus B’s velocity, both first measured in the same frame.

lessons.title: Acceleration changes velocity
lessons.idea: Acceleration tells us how velocity changes each second.
body: Choose a positive direction before using signs. A positive acceleration does not always mean speeding up. If velocity is negative, adding a positive change makes it less negative, so the object first slows down.

Constant acceleration means the same velocity change each second. Starting velocity v₀ plus acceleration a times elapsed time t gives current velocity v. For example, adding +2 m/s each second to −4 m/s reaches zero after 2 seconds.

The position rule has two changes: v₀t is what the starting velocity alone would contribute; ½at² is the extra displacement caused by the constant acceleration. Add both to starting position x₀. The half comes from the acceleration’s contribution growing steadily from zero during the interval.
lessons.equation: v = v₀ + at;   x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²
lessons.terms: v, v₀: Current and starting velocity (m/s). The subscript 0 means the chosen starting value. x, x₀: Current and starting position (m). Both use the same zero and direction. a: Constant acceleration (metres per second per second (m/s²)). The amount velocity changes in each second. t, ½, t²: Elapsed time, one half and time squared (s for t; s² for t²). t² means t multiplied by itself. Both v₀t and ½at² have units metres.

example.title: Slowing, then reversing
steps: Start with v₀ = −4 m/s and a = +2 m/s².
At t = 2 s: v = −4 m/s + (2 m/s²)(2 s) = 0 m/s.
At 3 s: v = +2 m/s. The direction has reversed.

visual.title: A changing velocity
visual.caption: Exact constant-acceleration equations. The displayed motion is one-dimensional and has no collisions.

check.prompt: An object has v = +6 m/s and a = −2 m/s². Over the next second, before reversal, what happens?
explanations: The acceleration is negative, so it reduces this positive velocity.
Negative acceleration does not instantly make velocity negative.
Yes. Velocity v = 6 m/s + (−2 m/s²)(1 s) = 4 m/s. It still moves in the positive direction.

apply.title: Estimate a stopping distance
apply.text: A cart at 4 m/s brakes uniformly at −2 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?
apply.answer: Let starting velocity v₀ be +4 m/s and acceleration a be −2 m/s². Each second removes 2 m/s, so stopping takes t = 2 s. Starting from x₀ = 0, displacement is (4 m/s)(2 s) + ½(−2 m/s²)(2 s)² = 8 m − 4 m = 4 m. This excludes reaction time and assumes constant braking acceleration.

lessons.limits: These equations require constant acceleration. Real braking depends on conditions; this is not a safety specification.

equationGuide.meaning: Final velocity is starting velocity plus its accumulated change. Final position is starting position plus the starting-velocity contribution and the extra constant-acceleration contribution.

lessons.title: Derive the constant-acceleration equations
lessons.idea: If velocity gains the same amount each second, we can calculate both velocity and position.
body: Constant acceleration means velocity changes by the same amount every second. Acceleration a is the rate dv/dt. Adding that rate over elapsed time gives v = v₀ + at: starting velocity plus its change.

Position change is velocity added over time. Integrating the changing velocity gives Δx = v₀t + ½at². The first part is the displacement you would get from the starting velocity alone; the second is the extra displacement caused by acceleration.

Combining the two rules removes time and gives v² = v₀² + 2aΔx. Squaring loses the direction sign, so a square root alone cannot tell you which way the object is moving. Use the event and motion conditions to choose the sign.
lessons.equation: v = v₀ + at;  Δx = v₀t + ½at²;  v² = v₀² + 2aΔx
lessons.terms: v, v₀: Final and starting velocity (m/s). The subscript 0 means the value at the chosen start t = 0. a: Constant acceleration (m/s²). Velocity change in metres per second, each second. t: Elapsed time (s). Time since the chosen start. Δx, x₀: Displacement and starting position (m). Δx = x − x₀; x is final position. ½ means one half; a square means multiply by itself.

example.title: Distance without time
steps: A cart has v₀ = 2 m/s, a = 1.5 m/s² and Δx = 4 m.
For this forward-accelerating branch, v = +4 m/s.

visual.title: Derive the constant-acceleration equations
visual.caption: Different equations answer different unknowns but share the same constant-a assumption.

check.prompt: Why is the position term ½at² rather than at²?
options: The object travels for only half the time
The added velocity grows from zero to at over the interval
Acceleration acts for only half the time
explanations: The whole elapsed interval contributes.
Yes. The extra velocity–time area is a triangle with area ½×t×at.
Acceleration acts throughout; the factor comes from integration.

apply.title: Check by differentiating
apply.text: Differentiate x = x₀+v₀t+½at² twice.
apply.answer: With x and x₀ in metres, v₀ in m/s, a in m/s² and t in seconds, the first time derivative of x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² is velocity v₀ + at. Differentiating once more gives acceleration a. This confirms the two rates agree with the assumed constant acceleration.

lessons.limits: Do not use these formulas unchanged for time-dependent acceleration. A constant numerical value in an equation must reflect a valid physical assumption.

equationGuide.meaning: The first rule finds final velocity, the second finds displacement, and the third relates velocity to displacement without using elapsed time. All require constant acceleration.

lessons.title: Use conditions to choose the physical solution
lessons.idea: Before solving for a time, say exactly which event you are looking for.
body: An object can pass the same place more than once. A tossed ball may cross a height on the way up and again on the way down. Both times can solve the position equation, but the question may ask for only one crossing.
Stopping means velocity is zero. It does not mean position is zero. Reaching a marker means position equals the marker position; the object might still be moving.

A root is a value that makes an equation true. Choose a root using the requested event and time interval, not just because it is convenient. Also check that the physical model still applies at that time.
lessons.equation: Stop condition: v(t) = 0;  marker condition: x(t) = x_marker
lessons.terms: t: Time (s). The time being tested for the event. v(t): Velocity at time t (m/s). v(t) = 0 means the object is momentarily at rest in this frame. x(t), x_marker: Object and marker positions (m). The same zero and positive axis must be used for both positions.

example.title: A reversal before the finish
steps: Let t be elapsed time in seconds and x position in metres. Starting at x₀ = 0, use x(t) = (4 m/s)t − (1 m/s²)t².
Its time derivative is velocity v(t) = 4 m/s − (2 m/s²)t. At t = 2 s this is zero and position is 4 m: the object stops momentarily.
At t = 4 s the position is back to 0 m, but velocity is −4 m/s. Returning and stopping are different events.

visual.title: Use conditions to choose the physical solution
visual.caption: Three events have different conditions and can occur at different times.

check.prompt: For the example, what is velocity when the object returns at t = 4 s?
explanations: The object stops at the turning point, not when it returns to the start.
It is moving in the negative direction on return.

apply.title: Reject an irrelevant root
apply.text: A motion equation gives times −2 s and +5 s for an event after the chosen start. Which root is relevant?
apply.answer: The +5 s root is in the requested interval t≥0. The negative root may describe the mathematical extension before the initial time, not a second future event.

lessons.limits: Only discard a root for a stated physical reason. Two positive roots can both be real events, and a model may cease to apply before either one.

equationGuide.meaning: To find a stop, set velocity to zero. To find arrival at a marker, set the object’s position equal to the marker position.

lessons.title: Accumulate a changing acceleration
lessons.idea: When acceleration changes, add the changes it produces rather than using its final value for the whole trip.
body: Acceleration tells us how quickly velocity changes. If acceleration varies with time, split time into small pieces and add acceleration times each short duration. An integral is the continuous version of that sum.

The integral from 0 to t adds the velocity change since the start. Add the starting velocity v₀ to find the current velocity. To find displacement, integrate that resulting velocity over time as a second step.

Using only the final acceleration times the full duration usually gives the wrong change. Units can be correct while the reasoning is wrong: the rate did not stay at its final value for the whole interval.
lessons.equation: v(t) = v₀ + ∫₀ᵗ a(s) ds
lessons.terms: v(t), v₀: Current and starting velocity (m/s). v(t) can vary with time. a(s): Acceleration at the running time s (m/s²). Here s is a temporary variable naming time inside the integral, not the seconds unit symbol. ∫₀ᵗ … ds: Integral from start to time t (adds m/s² × s to give m/s). The limits 0 and t specify the interval. ds tells us to add over time.

example.title: A ramped acceleration
steps: Let a(t) = (2 m/s³)t, with v₀ = 1 m/s.
Integrating gives v(t) = 1 m/s + (1 m/s³)t².
At t = 2 s, velocity is 5 m/s. Multiplying final acceleration 4 m/s² by 2 s would overestimate the change.

visual.title: Accumulate a changing acceleration
visual.caption: The area under the acceleration graph is velocity change. A linearly rising acceleration gives a triangular area.

check.prompt: For that model with x₀ = 0, what is displacement after 3 s?
explanations: The velocity at 3 s is 10 m/s; it is not the displacement.
Multiplying final velocity by total time ignores the earlier slower motion.
Yes. Integrate v: x = (1 m/s)t + (1/3 m/s³)t³. At 3 s, x = 3+9 = 12 m.

apply.title: Check an acceleration record
apply.text: How would you estimate velocity change from sampled acceleration measurements?
apply.answer: Add acceleration × short interval duration over the record, using a stated numerical integration rule. Include calibration and timing uncertainty; accumulating bias can produce substantial drift.

lessons.limits: Numerical integration accuracy depends on sampling, noise, bias and the integration method. This analytic example assumes the stated acceleration law is exact.

practice.prompt: Use a(t) = (3 m/s³)t with v(0)=2 m/s and x(0)=0. Evaluate at t=2 s.

parts.label: Velocity
parts.feedback: Integrate: v(t)=2 m/s +(1.5 m/s³)t². At 2 s this is 8 m/s.

parts.label: Position
parts.feedback: Integrate again: x(t)=(2 m/s)t +(0.5 m/s³)t³. At 2 s this is 4+4 = 8 m.

practice.reasoning: Instantaneous acceleration, accumulated velocity and accumulated position have different units and cannot be substituted for one another.

equationGuide.meaning: Current velocity equals starting velocity plus all the acceleration contributions accumulated from the start to the chosen time.

lessons.title: Split a launch into two directions
lessons.idea: A thrown object moves sideways and vertically at the same time, but gravity changes only the vertical motion in this model.
body: A component is the part of motion along one direction. Choose x horizontal, y upward, and put horizontal zero at launch. Ignore air resistance and use constant downward gravity near Earth’s surface.

Horizontal velocity then stays constant. Multiply its starting value vₓ by elapsed time t to find horizontal position. Vertically, start at height y₀, add the contribution vᵧt from initial upward velocity, then subtract ½gt² for gravity.

Here g is the positive size of gravitational acceleration: 9.81 metres per second each second. The minus sign gives its downward direction. At the top, vertical velocity is zero for a moment, but downward acceleration continues. Sideways motion need not stop.
lessons.equation: x = vₓt;   y = y₀ + vᵧt − ½gt²
lessons.terms: x, y, y₀: Horizontal position, height and starting height (m). x starts at zero; upward y is positive. vₓ, vᵧ: Starting horizontal and vertical velocity components (m/s). These symbols name the initial values. The horizontal value stays constant; the current vertical velocity later changes. g: Gravitational acceleration magnitude (m/s²). The model uses g = 9.81 m/s². Gravity’s vertical acceleration is −g. t, ½gt²: Elapsed time and gravity displacement contribution (s, m). ½ means half and t² means time multiplied by itself.

example.title: A horizontal launch
steps: Launch horizontally at vₓ = 3 m/s from height y₀ = 1.22625 m above the level floor. The initial vertical velocity vᵧ is zero.
Landing means y = 0. The vertical rule then gives ½gt² = y₀, so t = √(2y₀/g). With g = 9.81 m/s², t = √(0.25 s²) = 0.5 s. Choose the positive time.
During that half second, horizontal displacement is x = vₓt = (3 m/s)(0.5 s) = 1.5 m.

visual.title: One launch, two motions
visual.caption: Ideal trajectory for equal launch and landing heights; no air drag, uniform g = 9.81 m/s². Dots represent equal time steps, not measurements.

check.prompt: At the highest point of an angled ideal projectile, which quantity is zero?
explanations: For a nonvertical launch without drag, horizontal velocity stays constant and nonzero.
Yes. The vertical motion reverses there; downward acceleration remains g.
Gravity continues to act, so vertical acceleration is −g.

apply.title: Compare two drops
apply.text: One ball is released from rest while another is launched horizontally from the same height at the same instant. With no drag, which reaches the level floor first?
apply.answer: They arrive together. Both have the same initial vertical velocity and vertical acceleration. Their horizontal motions differ, but their vertical equations are identical.

lessons.limits: No air drag, no lift, constant g and locally flat ground. Not suitable for long-range ballistics or precise real-world safety decisions.

equationGuide.meaning: Horizontal position is horizontal velocity times time. Vertical position is starting height plus the initial-velocity contribution minus the growing downward change caused by gravity.

lessons.title: Include the launch height
lessons.idea: A projectile’s flight ends when its height reaches the actual landing surface.
body: Choose upward as positive and put height zero at the landing surface. A projectile starts at height y₀ with vertical velocity vᵧ₀. Constant downward gravity then gives height y = y₀ + vᵧ₀t − ½gt².

Set y to zero to find landing. Solve for time and select the relevant crossing. For a launch on or above the surface, the displayed plus-square-root expression gives a nonnegative landing time. It is a later crossing if the starting height is positive, or if the launch starts at surface level and points upward. At surface level with zero or downward vertical velocity, it gives t = 0: there is no later flight above that surface.

With no drag, horizontal velocity vₓ₀ stays constant, so horizontal range is vₓ₀ times landing time. The shortcut 2vᵧ₀/g for flight time assumes equal launch and landing heights; it does not generally work from a platform.
lessons.equation: t_land = [vᵧ₀ + √(vᵧ₀² + 2gy₀)]/g
lessons.terms: t_land: Landing time (s). The nonnegative crossing time. It is zero for a surface-level start with nonpositive vertical velocity. y₀: Starting height above landing surface (m). This formula assumes y₀ ≥ 0, meaning on or above that surface. vᵧ₀, vₓ₀: Starting vertical and horizontal velocity (m/s). Upward is positive for the vertical component. g: Magnitude of gravitational acceleration (m/s²). A positive number; the downward direction enters the minus sign in the height equation. Example g = 9.81 m/s².

example.title: A horizontal launch from a ledge
steps: Use y₀ = 4.905 m, vᵧ₀ = 0 and vₓ₀ = 2 m/s.
The fall time is √(2y₀/g) = 1 s.
The horizontal range is 2 m.

visual.title: Include the launch height
visual.caption: Vertical motion fixes the time; horizontal motion uses that same time.

check.prompt: From the same height with zero initial vertical speed, you double horizontal launch speed. With no drag, how does fall time change?
explanations: Horizontal motion does not shorten the vertical fall in this model.
Yes. The vertical equation is unchanged.
Horizontal speed does not enter this ideal vertical equation.

apply.title: State the landing condition
apply.text: A projectile lands on a platform above its launch point. Is the displayed y₀≥0 formula directly the right setup?
apply.answer: Not without redefining the coordinates and checking reachability. Write the actual landing height into y(t)=y_land, solve, and choose the relevant future crossing.

lessons.limits: No drag or lift, uniform downward gravity and a locally flat frame. The model does not establish safe real-world launch trajectories.

equationGuide.meaning: Solve for when vertical position reaches the landing height. This plus-square-root branch gives a nonnegative time. At surface level without an upward launch, it gives zero, not a later flight.

lessons.title: Resolve the launch before calculating the range
lessons.idea: A steeper launch gives more upward motion but less horizontal motion at the same starting speed.
body: The launch angle θ is measured above horizontal. Sine and cosine split starting speed v₀ into components: vₓ₀ = v₀ cos θ horizontally and vᵧ₀ = v₀ sin θ upward. Use the angle mode matching your numbers.

For equal launch and landing heights, no air resistance and constant downward gravity, the upward component determines time in the air. Multiplying flight time by the horizontal component gives range R = v₀² sin(2θ)/g.

With these assumptions and fixed starting speed, the largest range is at 45°. Different heights, air resistance, lift or a changing launch speed can change that answer. This is a model result, not a universal launching rule.
lessons.equation: R = v₀² sin(2θ)/g  (equal heights, no drag)
lessons.terms: R: Horizontal range (m). Horizontal distance from launch to the same-height landing point. v₀: Starting speed (m/s). A nonnegative magnitude, not one component. θ: Launch angle (degrees or radians consistently). The example uses degrees; sin(2θ) means sine of twice the angle, not twice its sine. g: Gravitational acceleration magnitude (m/s²). The example uses the rounded positive value 9.8 m/s².

example.title: Complementary launch angles
steps: Use v₀ = 7 m/s and g = 9.8 m/s² as a rounded example.
At θ = 60°, sin120° = sin60°, so the ideal range is the same; the flight time differs.

visual.title: Resolve the launch before calculating the range
visual.caption: Equal range does not imply equal trajectories or flight times. This symmetry requires the stated ideal conditions.

check.prompt: At fixed angle and the same ideal assumptions, doubling launch speed changes range by what factor?
explanations: Yes. The range depends on v₀².
Both the horizontal speed and flight time grow with launch speed.
Increasing speed does not reduce the range in this model.

apply.title: Check the 45° rule
apply.text: Why should a real ball launched from an elevated platform not automatically be assigned a 45° optimum?
apply.answer: The equal-height assumption fails, and drag may also matter. Optimize the actual height-and-drag model rather than importing the simplified conclusion.

lessons.limits: The 45° result is for a uniform-g, no-drag, equal-height model with fixed initial speed and no terrain obstacles.

practice.prompt: In an ideal equal-height launch, use v₀=6 m/s, θ=45° and rounded g=9 m/s².
practice.reasoning: All three predictions assume no drag, uniform g and the stated launch/landing geometry. A real launch is not guaranteed to follow them.

equationGuide.meaning: Square the starting speed, multiply by the sine of twice the launch angle, then divide by gravitational acceleration to get horizontal range in this ideal equal-height case.

lessons.title: Newton’s first law selects a kind of frame
lessons.idea: In an inertial frame, zero net force means unchanged velocity—not necessarily rest.
body: An inertial frame is a viewpoint in which an object with no net external force keeps a constant velocity. Net force means the directed total of all external forces. Constant velocity can be zero, or it can be steady motion in a fixed direction.
A frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial in classical mechanics. Two such observers may disagree about velocity but agree that the velocity is not changing.

An accelerating or rotating viewpoint is generally different. It can make a free object appear to accelerate. Newton-style equations then need extra frame-related terms, which are outside this first frame model.
lessons.equation: ΣF = 0 → a = 0 → v is constant  (in an inertial frame)
lessons.terms: ΣF: Net external force (newtons (N)). Σ means add all the directed force contributions. a: Acceleration (m/s²). Rate of velocity change. v: Velocity (m/s). Unchanged velocity is not required to be zero. →: Implication (not a quantity). Here the arrow means “therefore”, not a force direction.

example.title: Two descriptions of a free cart
steps: In a lab frame, a cart moves at 2 m/s with zero net force.
In a frame moving alongside at 2 m/s, it is at rest.
Both descriptions have zero acceleration and satisfy the first law.

visual.title: Newton’s first law selects a kind of frame
visual.caption: Constant relative frame velocity changes the velocity value, not whether acceleration is zero.

check.prompt: A car brakes while a loose low-friction object keeps moving forward relative to the ground. What needs care?
options: The object must have a new forward force
Newton’s first law requires the object to stop
The braking car frame is accelerating
explanations: A continuing ground-frame velocity need not require a forward net force.
The first law predicts constant velocity, not automatic rest.
Yes. Relative to the decelerating car, the object appears to move forward even without a new forward force.

apply.title: Choose a modelling frame
apply.text: Why is a stationary laboratory often treated as approximately inertial for a short tabletop experiment?
apply.answer: Earth’s rotation and orbital motion usually produce negligible corrections at that scale and precision. The approximation must be reconsidered for long duration, large scales or sensitive measurements.

lessons.limits: No terrestrial laboratory is exactly inertial. The acceptable approximation depends on the experiment’s scale and required accuracy.

equationGuide.meaning: Add the external forces. If their total is zero in an inertial frame, acceleration is zero and velocity stays constant.

symbols.name: Net external force
symbols.description: Σ means add all the directed force contributions.

symbols.name: Acceleration
symbols.description: Rate of velocity change.

symbols.name: Velocity

symbols.name: Implication
symbols.description: Here the arrow means “therefore”, not a force direction.

Coming from outside the chosen object or system.

lessons.title: Add the forces before predicting motion
lessons.idea: Add the forces before deciding how velocity will change.
body: Force is a push or pull from an interaction. Several can act at once. Add their signed components in each direction to get the net force: the combined effect. Equal opposing forces cancel in this sum, even though each force is still present.

An inertial frame is a viewpoint in which a free object keeps constant velocity. For constant mass in such a frame, acceleration equals net force divided by mass. A newton is the force unit: one newton gives a one-kilogram mass acceleration of one metre per second each second.

Zero net force therefore means zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity. The object may stay at rest or keep moving steadily in the same direction. A force is needed to change that velocity, not to maintain it.
lessons.equation: ΣF = ma
lessons.terms: ΣF: Net external force (newtons (N)). Σ, read sigma, means add. External means coming from outside the chosen object. m: Constant mass (kilograms (kg)). The amount of mass in the object. a: Acceleration (m/s²). Rate of velocity change, including direction. 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²: Newton unit definition (force). A dot between unit symbols means multiply: kilogram times metre per second squared.

example.title: Two pushes on a cart
steps: A 3 kg cart receives +10 N and −4 N horizontally.
Net horizontal force = +6 N.
Horizontal acceleration = (6 N) ÷ (3 kg) = +2 m/s². The velocity changes by +2 m/s each second while that net force continues.

visual.title: Net force is the combined effect
visual.caption: Horizontal forces on a constant-mass object. Vertical forces are assumed to balance; friction is included only if represented by a control.

check.prompt: A cart moves right at constant velocity. Its net force is zero. What happens next in this model?
explanations: Yes. Zero net force gives zero acceleration, not zero velocity.
Stopping would require a change in velocity and therefore a nonzero net force.
Acceleration would require a nonzero net force.

apply.title: Choose what to measure
apply.text: You double a constant-mass cart's net force. What happens to its acceleration?
apply.answer: It doubles in the same direction: a = Fnet/m. Its velocity does not instantly double; velocity changes over time under that acceleration.

lessons.limits: Newton's second law in this form assumes constant mass and an inertial frame. Relativistic speeds and quantum-scale behaviour need other descriptions.

equationGuide.meaning: The directed sum of external forces equals mass multiplied by acceleration. Divide by mass to find acceleration from the net force.

lessons.title: Keep action–reaction forces on different objects
lessons.idea: Two interacting objects exert equal and opposite forces on each other.
body: When A pushes B, B pushes A with the same force size in the opposite direction, in this classical contact model. One force acts on A and the other on B. They do not cancel in the force total for either object alone.
The same force size can cause different accelerations. Acceleration is net force divided by mass, so the smaller mass changes velocity more quickly when other forces do not alter the comparison.

If both objects are counted together as one system, their mutual forces are internal: they act between members. Those equal and opposite terms cancel when the two force equations are added. Outside forces still matter.
lessons.equation: F_A on B = −F_B on A
lessons.terms: F_A on B: Force exerted by A on B (N). This force belongs in B’s force equation. F_B on A: Force exerted by B on A (N). This force belongs in A’s force equation. −: Opposite vector (not a unit). The minus reverses direction; it does not mean a negative force magnitude.

example.title: Two carts push apart
steps: Cart A has mass 2 kg and cart B mass 5 kg. The interaction magnitude is 10 N.
A’s acceleration magnitude is 10/2 = 5 m/s².
B’s is 10/5 = 2 m/s², in the opposite direction.

visual.title: Keep action–reaction forces on different objects
visual.caption: Equal and opposite forces can produce unequal accelerations because the masses differ.

check.prompt: A book rests on a table. Is the table’s upward force on the book the third-law partner of Earth’s downward force on the book?
options: Yes; every balanced pair is a third-law pair
No; both act on the book
explanations: Balanced forces on one body are not the two forces of a third-law interaction pair.
Yes. The partner of Earth-on-book gravity is book-on-Earth gravity. The partner of table-on-book contact acts on the table.
Equal magnitude alone does not identify an interaction pair.

apply.title: Choose a system
apply.text: Why do the two carts’ mutual push forces disappear when summing the momentum equations for both carts?
apply.answer: Adding the two objects’ force equations cancels their internal, equal-and-opposite pushes. The remaining outside forces control how the combined motion changes. Later, momentum—mass times velocity—provides another way to express that same combined balance.

lessons.limits: This pairwise classical statement must be supplemented by field momentum for a complete treatment of some electromagnetic interactions. The present examples use ordinary mechanical contacts.

practice.prompt: Two carts push apart. A has mass 3 kg and receives +12 N; B has mass 6 kg. Ignore other horizontal forces.

parts.label: Force on B
parts.feedback: The interaction pair gives the same magnitude in the opposite direction.

practice.reasoning: Equal force magnitudes do not imply equal acceleration magnitudes; mass matters. The forces act on different carts.

equationGuide.meaning: The force A exerts on B is equal in size and opposite in direction to the force B exerts on A.

symbols.name: Force exerted by A on B
symbols.description: This force belongs in B’s force equation.

symbols.name: Force exerted by B on A
symbols.description: This force belongs in A’s force equation.

symbols.name: Opposite vector
symbols.description: The minus reverses direction; it does not mean a negative force magnitude.

glossary.definition: The two forces the interacting objects exert on one another.
A force between parts of the chosen system.

lessons.title: Draw only the forces acting on your chosen system
lessons.idea: Choose what you are studying before drawing its force arrows.
body: The system is the object or group you choose to study. Draw it separately. A free-body diagram shows forces from outside that system acting on it. Name the source of each force.

Do not include a force the system exerts on another object as though it acted back on itself. For a box alone, Earth pulls the box down and a table pushes it up. The box’s downward push on the table acts on the table, not the box.
For a group, forces between its members are internal and cancel from the combined force total. A different system boundary can simplify the calculation without changing the real interactions.

For several objects, the corresponding combined equation uses total mass and acceleration of the centre of mass—the mass-weighted average position taught later. The single-body examples here do not require that later calculation.
lessons.equation: ΣF_external = m a  for a constant-mass single body
lessons.terms: ΣF_external: Net external force (N). Σ means add directed forces acting on the system from outside. m: Mass (kilograms (kg)). Constant in this equation. a: Acceleration (m/s²). A vector, so each direction has its own force balance.

example.title: A box pulled across a table
steps: Choose the box alone. Its forces include gravity from Earth, contact from the table and a pull from a rope.
If sliding friction is relevant, include it along the surface opposite relative sliding.
Do not add the box’s downward push on the table to the box diagram.

visual.title: Draw only the forces acting on your chosen system
visual.caption: Each arrow needs both a receiving system and an external source. A diagram is a force inventory, not a motion picture.

check.prompt: You choose two connected carts as one system. Is their mutual connector force external?
options: Yes; every contact force is external
Only if the carts are moving
explanations: Yes. Both interacting carts are inside the chosen boundary.
External versus internal depends on the system boundary, not force type.
Motion does not decide whether the interaction crosses the boundary.

apply.title: Audit a diagram
apply.text: What question should you ask when you see an unlabeled force arrow?
apply.answer: “Which external object exerts this force on my chosen system?” If no interaction can be identified, the arrow may be an invented extra force or a mislabeled effect.

lessons.limits: A free-body diagram is incomplete until relevant contacts, fields and model assumptions have been considered. Omitting a small force is an approximation that should be justified.

equationGuide.meaning: For one constant-mass body in an inertial frame, the directed total of external forces equals mass times acceleration.

symbols.description: Σ means add directed forces acting on the system from outside.

symbols.name: Mass
symbols.description: Constant in this equation.

symbols.description: A vector, so each direction has its own force balance.

lessons.title: Do not assume contact forces equal weight
lessons.idea: A surface pushes perpendicular to itself; a taut ideal rope pulls along its length.
body: Normal means perpendicular, or at a right angle to the surface. The normal force is the surface’s push on the object. Its size follows from the motion and the other forces; it is not always equal to weight.

For a box touching a horizontal table with no vertical acceleration, upward forces balance downward forces. If weight is mg and an extra upward pull is F_up, the table only needs to supply the rest: N + F_up − mg = 0.

Tension is the pulling force along a taut rope. Taut means pulled tight, not slack. An ideal massless rope carries equal tension along a straight segment; a massless frictionless pulley can turn the rope without changing that tension. Real rope mass and pulley friction can change this model.
lessons.equation: Vertical balance example: N + F_up − mg = 0
lessons.terms: N: Normal force (newtons (N)). The italic-style quantity name N and upright unit N look alike here; a number followed by N means newtons. F_up: Added upward force (N). An extra pull, such as a hand partly supporting the box. m, g: Mass and gravitational acceleration magnitude (kg, m/s²). Their product mg is weight in newtons. Zero on the right means zero net vertical force.

example.title: Partly support a box
steps: A 2 kg box rests on a table. Use g = 10 m/s² for this rounded example.
An external hand pulls upward with 6 N.
N = 20−6 = 14 N while contact is maintained.

visual.title: Do not assume contact forces equal weight
visual.caption: The contact force supplies the remaining vertical balance. It is not fixed independently at mg.

check.prompt: In the example, increasing the upward pull to 10 N while the box remains at rest changes N to what?
explanations: That ignores the additional upward force.
An upward pull reduces, rather than increases, the required normal force here.

apply.title: Recognize loss of contact
apply.text: If a force-balance calculation asks a nonadhesive table to exert a downward normal force on a box above it, what should you do?
apply.answer: Reconsider the assumed contact. A simple nonadhesive surface can push but not pull the box downward; the box may lift off and require a different motion model.

lessons.limits: The ideal tension statements assume negligible rope and pulley mass as specified. Contact forces may be distributed, but this particle model replaces them with resultants.

equationGuide.meaning: In this vertical balance, the table’s upward push plus the added upward pull equals downward weight.

symbols.description: The italic-style quantity name N and upright unit N look alike here; a number followed by N means newtons.

symbols.name: Added upward force
symbols.description: An extra pull, such as a hand partly supporting the box.

symbols.description: Their product mg is weight in newtons. Zero on the right means zero net vertical force.

A pulling force along a connector such as a rope.
Pulled tight, without slack.

lessons.title: Choose axes that simplify the constraint
lessons.idea: Split gravity into a part down the slope and a part pressing into the slope.
body: Choose one axis along the ramp and one perpendicular to it. The ramp angle θ is measured from horizontal. Gravity still points straight down, but its components in these axes are mg sin θ down the ramp and mg cos θ into it.
If no other perpendicular force acts and the object does not accelerate through the surface, the normal force balances the into-surface component: N = mg cos θ.
On a frictionless slope, the down-slope force is mg sin θ. Divide by mass to get acceleration a = g sin θ. The mass cancels: this ideal sliding acceleration does not depend on the object’s mass.
lessons.equation: F_gravity,parallel = mg sinθ;  N = mg cosθ
lessons.terms: F_gravity,parallel: Down-slope gravity component (N). Positive is chosen down the slope. N: Normal force (N). The perpendicular surface push. m, g: Mass and gravitational acceleration magnitude (kg, m/s²). mg is the weight in newtons. θ: Ramp angle above horizontal (degrees in the example). Sine and cosine give the shares in the chosen right-angle directions; use matching calculator mode.

example.title: A frictionless 30° slope
steps: Use m = 2 kg and rounded g = 10 m/s².
Downslope gravity = 20 sin30° = 10 N.
Acceleration = 10/2 = 5 m/s². Normal force is 20 cos30° ≈ 17.32 N.

visual.title: Choose axes that simplify the constraint
visual.caption: The components are a decomposition of one gravity force, not extra forces added on top of gravity.

check.prompt: What does the frictionless downslope acceleration become as θ approaches zero?
explanations: There is no singularity in g sinθ at zero.
Yes. sin0 = 0, matching a horizontal surface.
g corresponds to the vertical-slope limit in this ideal model.

apply.title: Check a limiting case
apply.text: Why is the vertical-slope limit useful for checking the formula?
apply.answer: As θ approaches 90°, sinθ approaches 1 and cosθ approaches 0. The acceleration approaches g and the required normal force approaches zero, consistent with loss of sideways support.

lessons.limits: No friction or other forces in the acceleration formula. The object is treated as sliding, not rolling; rotational motion requires another model.

equationGuide.meaning: The sine part of weight acts down the ramp. The cosine part presses into it and is balanced by the normal force under the stated contact conditions.

symbols.description: Positive is chosen down the slope.

symbols.description: mg is the weight in newtons.

lessons.title: Use the constraint to connect accelerations
lessons.idea: A tight rope that does not stretch can make two carts share one acceleration.
body: Inextensible means unable to stretch in this model. A taut, fixed-length rope between two carts moving along one straight line keeps their separation fixed. Their along-line accelerations must then match.

Treat both carts together first. Their mutual rope pulls are internal and cancel from the combined force total. Divide the total outside horizontal force by total mass to find the common acceleration.
Then consider the rear cart alone. Its forward rope tension must give that cart its acceleration. This second step finds tension; the whole-system equation alone cannot tell you the internal pull.
lessons.equation: a = F_external/(m₁ + m₂)  for the stated frictionless two-cart setup
lessons.terms: a: Common acceleration (m/s²). Both carts share it because of this fixed-length straight-line rope geometry. F_external: Net external horizontal pull (N). Applied to the leading cart here; the internal rope pulls cancel in the combined system. m₁, m₂: Cart masses (kg). The subscripts 1 and 2 label the carts; add the masses before dividing.

example.title: Pull two connected carts
steps: A rear cart has mass m₁ = 2 kg and a front cart has mass m₂ = 3 kg. A 10 N horizontal pull acts on the front cart; friction is ignored.
Common acceleration a = 10 N ÷ (2 kg + 3 kg) = 2 m/s².
The rear cart needs tension T = m₁a = (2 kg)(2 m/s²) = 4 N. For the front cart, net force is 10 N − 4 N = 6 N, matching (3 kg)(2 m/s²).

visual.title: Use the constraint to connect accelerations
visual.caption: The system boundary removes internal tension for the total equation, but each cart still experiences it.

check.prompt: In this setup, why is tension not 10 N?
options: Some of the pull accelerates the front cart as well
The rope loses 6 N to friction
explanations: Yes. The external pull accelerates both carts; the connector transmits the force needed for the rear cart.
The stated ideal rope has no frictional loss.
The connector’s interaction pair remains equal and opposite.

apply.title: Test the system equation
apply.text: If the rear cart mass increases while the same pull is applied, what happens to the common acceleration?
apply.answer: It decreases because the total mass increases. The tension must be recalculated from the rear cart’s mass times the new acceleration.

lessons.limits: The equal-acceleration constraint is geometry-specific. Moving pulleys, slack rope or stretching can give different relations.

practice.prompt: A 1.5 kg rear cart and 2.5 kg front cart are connected by a massless taut rope on a frictionless horizontal surface. A 12 N pull acts on the front cart.

parts.label: Common acceleration
parts.feedback: Total mass 4 kg gives a=12/4 =3 m/s².

parts.label: Rope tension
parts.feedback: The rear cart needs T=1.5×3 =4.5 N.

practice.reasoning: The connector force is internal for the pair but external for each cart considered alone.

equationGuide.meaning: For these frictionless connected carts, common acceleration equals the outside pull divided by the sum of the masses.

symbols.name: Common acceleration
symbols.description: Both carts share it because of this fixed-length straight-line rope geometry.

symbols.name: Net external horizontal pull
symbols.description: Applied to the leading cart here; the internal rope pulls cancel in the combined system.

symbols.name: Cart masses
symbols.description: The subscripts 1 and 2 label the carts; add the masses before dividing.

A condition linking the allowed motions.
The rope’s pulling force.

lessons.title: Static friction adjusts up to a limit
lessons.idea: When touching surfaces do not slide, friction adjusts to keep them from sliding—up to a limit.
body: Push a box gently and it can stay still. Static friction is the along-surface contact force that prevents relative sliding. Its size matches what the balance requires; it is not automatically at its maximum.

In a simple dry-contact model, that maximum is μₛN. Here N is the normal force pressing the surfaces together and μₛ is a dimensionless number describing the contact. The inequality |fₛ| ≤ μₛN means friction size is at most that maximum.

First find how much friction would be needed and which way it must act. Then compare with the maximum. Its direction opposes the relative sliding that would begin without it—not necessarily every motion relative to the floor.
lessons.equation: |fₛ| ≤ μₛN
lessons.terms: fₛ: Static friction (newtons (N)). The subscript s labels static friction; bars | | mean its nonnegative size. μₛ: Static-friction coefficient (no unit). Read mu-sub-s. A positive contact parameter, not a force. N: Normal-force magnitude (N). The perpendicular push between the surfaces; the repeated N is also the unit symbol for newtons. ≤: Less than or equal to (not a unit). This is a maximum, not a claim the force always equals it.

example.title: A gentle push
steps: A box has N = 20 N and μₛ = 0.4, so maximum static friction is 8 N.
You push horizontally with 5 N and the box remains at rest.
The friction magnitude is 5 N, opposite the push—not 8 N.

visual.title: Static friction adjusts up to a limit
visual.caption: Required balance is compared with a capacity. The inequality is not an automatic equality.

check.prompt: The horizontal push rises to 7 N while the same box remains at rest. What is static-friction magnitude?
explanations: Yes. It balances the required 7 N, still below the 8 N maximum.
8 N is the maximum, not the force in every stuck state.
The unused capacity is not the friction force.

apply.title: Find the threshold
apply.text: If the required tangential friction becomes 9 N but μₛN = 8 N, can this static state persist under the model?
apply.answer: No. Static friction cannot supply the required force. Relative sliding begins and the kinetic model, if applicable, must be used.

lessons.limits: This is an empirical idealized contact model. Surface conditions, vibration, deformation and adhesion can alter friction behaviour.

equationGuide.meaning: The size of static friction can be anything from zero up to the coefficient times the normal force, as the contact balance requires.

symbols.name: Static friction
symbols.description: The subscript s labels static friction; bars | | mean its nonnegative size.

symbols.name: Static-friction coefficient
symbols.description: Read mu-sub-s. A positive contact parameter, not a force.

symbols.name: Normal-force magnitude
symbols.description: The perpendicular push between the surfaces; the repeated N is also the unit symbol for newtons.

symbols.name: Less than or equal to
symbols.description: This is a maximum, not a claim the force always equals it.

glossary.definition: Contact friction while the surfaces are not sliding relative to each other.
A multiplying number in the model.
Along the surface rather than through it.

lessons.title: Sliding friction follows relative motion
lessons.idea: When surfaces slide against one another, friction opposes their relative sliding.
body: Kinetic friction means sliding friction. A common simple model gives its size as μₖN: the sliding-friction coefficient times the normal-force magnitude.

The coefficient μₖ is a unit-free number treated as constant over the limited conditions being studied. Real friction can depend on materials, temperature and speed; the formula is an approximation, not a universal contact law.
Use the sliding of one surface compared with the other to choose direction. A moving belt can pull a box forward relative to the floor while reducing the box’s backward sliding relative to the belt.
lessons.equation: |fₖ| = μₖN
lessons.terms: fₖ: Kinetic friction (N). Bars give its size. Its direction opposes the relative sliding of the surfaces. μₖ: Sliding-friction coefficient (no unit). Read mu-sub-k. Constant only within the stated approximation. N: Normal-force magnitude (N). The perpendicular contact push, measured in newtons.

example.title: A sliding box on a fixed floor
steps: A 2 kg box slides right with N = 20 N and μₖ = 0.3.
Friction is 6 N leftward.
If it is the only horizontal force, acceleration is −6/2 = −3 m/s².

visual.title: Sliding friction follows relative motion
visual.caption: A friction arrow opposes relative sliding at contact. This diagram assumes the floor is stationary.

check.prompt: A box at rest in the floor frame is placed on a belt moving right beneath it. Which way does sliding friction initially act on the box?
explanations: That would increase the relative sliding instead of opposing it.
There is relative motion at the contact even though the box starts at rest in the floor frame.
Yes. Relative to the belt, the box slides left, so belt-on-box friction acts right.

apply.title: Check an energy statement
apply.text: Can friction ever do positive work on an object in the floor frame?
apply.answer: Yes. Work is energy transferred by a force along the displacement of the object. A moving belt can exert a forward force on a box while the box moves forward in the floor frame, so its work on the box is positive. The belt’s drive supplies energy; the sliding contact can also produce heat.

lessons.limits: “Friction always slows an object in every frame” is incorrect. Dissipation concerns the full interacting system and relative motion.

equationGuide.meaning: Sliding-friction magnitude equals the sliding coefficient multiplied by normal-force magnitude in this contact model.

symbols.name: Kinetic friction
symbols.description: Bars give its size. Its direction opposes the relative sliding of the surfaces.

symbols.name: Sliding-friction coefficient
symbols.description: Read mu-sub-k. Constant only within the stated approximation.

symbols.name: Normal-force magnitude
symbols.description: The perpendicular contact push, measured in newtons.

glossary.definition: Friction during relative sliding.
Movement of one touching surface compared with the other.
Transfer of organized mechanical energy into less directly recoverable forms, such as heating.

lessons.title: Let resistance depend on velocity
lessons.idea: In a linear-drag model, doubling velocity relative to the surrounding material doubles the opposing drag force.
body: The surrounding material, such as air or water, is called the medium. Take it to be stationary in this frame. In one dimension, F_drag = −bv uses a positive constant b; the minus sign makes the force oppose the signed velocity v relative to the medium.

With constant mass and no other force, mass times velocity’s time derivative equals drag: m dv/dt = −bv. Its solution is v(t) = v₀e^(−t/τ), where τ = m/b. The constant e is about 2.718. Every time interval τ multiplies velocity by 1/e, about 0.368, instead of subtracting a fixed amount.

Power means the rate of work or energy transfer. For a one-dimensional force on this particle, P = Fv: force times velocity. Multiplying drag force by velocity tells us whether it adds or removes kinetic energy, the energy of motion.
lessons.equation: F_drag = −bv;  τ = m/b;  v(t) = v₀e^(−t/τ)
lessons.terms: F_drag: Drag force (N). Opposes velocity relative to the stationary medium. b: Linear drag coefficient (kilograms per second (kg/s)). Positive and constant in this model. v(t), v₀: Velocity now and at the start (m/s). Signed relative to the medium. m, τ, t: Mass, decay time and elapsed time (kg, s, s). τ, read tau, equals m/b. The ratio t/τ is unit-free. e^(−t/τ): Exponential factor (no unit). e is a fixed number about 2.718; this factor decreases with positive elapsed time.

example.title: A hypothetical damped glide
steps: Let m = 2 kg, b = 1 kg/s and v₀ = 3 m/s.
The time scale is τ = 2 s.
At t = 2 s, v = 3/e ≈ 1.10 m/s, still in the original direction.

visual.title: Let resistance depend on velocity
visual.caption: This model gives a fractional decrease over equal intervals. It approaches rest without reversing direction under drag alone.

check.prompt: If m doubles while b stays fixed, what happens to the decay time scale τ?
explanations: The mass explicitly appears in the time scale.
Yes. τ = m/b.
More inertia gives a slower response to the same drag coefficient.

apply.title: Check the power sign
apply.text: What is drag power F_drag v in this model?
apply.answer: Power P = F_drag v = −bv². Here P is in watts (joules per second), b is positive in kg/s, and v is in m/s. The square v² cannot be negative, so power is zero or negative: drag removes kinetic energy relative to this stationary medium. This conclusion uses the no-other-force setup.

lessons.limits: Linear drag is appropriate only in some flow regimes. Many everyday high-speed objects require a different drag law; the medium’s velocity must be included if it moves.

equationGuide.meaning: Drag is opposite to velocity. The ratio mass divided by drag coefficient gives a decay time; after that time, the no-other-force velocity is about 36.8 percent of its earlier value.

symbols.description: Opposes velocity relative to the stationary medium.

symbols.description: Positive and constant in this model.

symbols.description: Signed relative to the medium.

symbols.description: e is a fixed number about 2.718; this factor decreases with positive elapsed time.
