The time over which this exponential falls by a factor of e.
Energy transfer per unit time; measured in watts, or joules per second.

lessons.title: Terminal speed is a force balance
lessons.idea: At terminal speed, an object keeps falling even though its acceleration has fallen to zero.
body: Choose downward as positive. Weight mg pulls down; drag opposes the fall. With linear drag, the net force is mg − bv. At terminal speed these forces balance, so acceleration is zero but velocity need not be zero.

Setting mg − bv_t = 0 gives v_t = mg/b. The subscript t here means terminal, not multiplication by time. A different model has drag size cv² and gives v_t = √(mg/c) for downward motion. The correct law depends on the physical conditions or measurements.

Kinetic energy is energy of motion. For a constant-mass classical particle, K = ½mv²: half the mass times speed squared. K is in joules, m in kilograms and v in metres per second. A constant speed therefore means constant kinetic energy even while the object keeps losing height.
lessons.equation: Linear: v_t = mg/b;  quadratic: v_t = √(mg/c)
lessons.terms: v_t: Terminal speed (m/s). The positive downward speed at force balance. m, g: Mass and gravity magnitude (kg, m/s²). Their product mg is weight in newtons. b: Linear coefficient (kg/s). Positive; multiplies velocity in the linear force law. c: Quadratic coefficient (kg/m). Positive; multiplies speed squared in the quadratic force law. √: Square root (operator). Gives the nonnegative speed whose square matches the inside value.

example.title: A linear-drag fall
steps: Use m = 1 kg, g = 10 m/s² and b = 2 kg/s as rounded model values.
Set the net force to zero: 10−2v_t = 0.
Terminal speed is 5 m/s downward.

visual.title: Terminal speed is a force balance
visual.caption: Terminal does not mean stopped. It means opposing forces balance at a nonzero speed.

check.prompt: At terminal speed under constant gravity and the stated drag law, what is kinetic energy doing?
explanations: Yes. Constant mass and constant speed give constant kinetic energy.
Motion alone does not imply increasing kinetic energy.
The object has nonzero speed, so its kinetic energy is nonzero.

apply.title: Follow the energy
apply.text: If kinetic energy is constant during a terminal-speed fall, where does the lost gravitational potential energy go?
apply.answer: It is transferred to the object/medium through drag, ultimately including thermal energy and fluid motion. Energy is not disappearing.

lessons.limits: These formulas omit buoyancy and changes in density, orientation and drag coefficient. A real falling object may not reach a steady terminal regime.

practice.prompt: For downward motion use m=2 kg, g=10 m/s² and quadratic upward drag magnitude cv² with c=0.8 kg/m.

parts.label: Terminal speed
parts.feedback: Balance 20 N with 0.8 v²: v²=25, so downward speed 5 m/s.

parts.label: Downward acceleration at 3 m/s
parts.feedback: Net downward force 20−7.2=12.8 N; divide by 2 kg to get 6.4 m/s².

practice.reasoning: Below terminal speed, gravity exceeds drag in this model. At terminal speed they balance, without implying zero velocity.

equationGuide.meaning: Set downward weight equal to upward drag. Divide weight by the linear coefficient, or take the square root of weight divided by the quadratic coefficient, depending on the chosen drag law.

symbols.name: Terminal speed
symbols.description: The positive downward speed at force balance.

symbols.name: Mass and gravity magnitude
symbols.description: Their product mg is weight in newtons.

symbols.name: Linear coefficient
symbols.description: Positive; multiplies velocity in the linear force law.

symbols.name: Quadratic coefficient
symbols.description: Positive; multiplies speed squared in the quadratic force law.

symbols.name: Square root
symbols.description: Gives the nonnegative speed whose square matches the inside value.

glossary.definition: A steady speed reached or approached when the relevant forces balance.
Depending on a quantity squared.
The upward net force from pressure in a surrounding fluid; omitted in these formulas.

lessons.title: Changing direction is acceleration
lessons.idea: Moving around a circle changes velocity’s direction, even if speed stays the same.
body: Velocity includes direction. On a circle at constant speed, the direction of motion keeps turning. Acceleration is the rate of velocity change, so it is not zero.
For uniform circular motion, the acceleration points toward the centre. Its size is v²/r: speed squared divided by radius. Radial means along the line between the object and the centre.

The velocity points along the tangent—the straight line that just touches the circle at that place. Inward acceleration is at a right angle to this velocity. It changes direction without changing speed in this uniform case.
lessons.equation: a_radial = v²/r = ω²r
lessons.terms: a_radial: Inward acceleration magnitude (m/s²). A nonnegative size; its direction is toward the centre. v, r: Speed and radius (m/s, m). The circle has positive radius. ω: Angular speed (radians per second (rad/s)). Read omega. ω = v/r counts turning angle per second; radians are dimensionless in the unit calculation.

example.title: A circular track model
steps: A cart moves at 3 m/s around a circle of radius 1.5 m.
Radial acceleration magnitude is 9/1.5 = 6 m/s².
Its speed can remain 3 m/s while the velocity vector changes.

visual.title: Changing direction is acceleration
visual.caption: Velocity is tangent; radial acceleration is inward. Arrows describe different physical quantities.

check.prompt: At the same radius, doubling speed changes radial acceleration by what factor?
explanations: Acceleration depends quadratically, not linearly, on speed here.
Increasing speed increases the required radial acceleration.
Yes. The speed is squared in v²/r.

apply.title: Release the constraint
apply.text: If the inward force suddenly vanishes, which direction does the object initially move in an inertial frame?
apply.answer: Along its instantaneous tangent velocity, not straight outward from the centre. Without another force it continues along that tangent line.

lessons.limits: The formula assumes motion along a circle of known radius. For a general curve, use the local radius of curvature and account for tangential acceleration separately.

equationGuide.meaning: Inward acceleration equals speed squared divided by radius. The equivalent angular form uses angular speed squared times radius.

symbols.name: Inward acceleration magnitude
symbols.description: A nonnegative size; its direction is toward the centre.

symbols.name: Speed and radius
symbols.description: The circle has positive radius.

symbols.name: Angular speed
symbols.description: Read omega. ω = v/r counts turning angle per second; radians are dimensionless in the unit calculation.

glossary.definition: Along a centre-to-object line.
A straight line touching the circle at one place, perpendicular to its radius there.
Motion around a fixed-radius circle at constant speed.

lessons.title: Centripetal is a role, not an extra force
lessons.idea: Real forces must add up to the inward force needed for the circular motion.
body: Centripetal means centre-seeking. “Centripetal force” names the net inward force requirement; it is not an extra interaction to add beside gravity, tension or friction.
Choose inward as positive and add the components of actual forces along that direction. Their total must equal mv²/r, because mass times inward acceleration gives the required force.
Force components along the tangent change speed and need a separate balance. If actual forces cannot supply the required inward total, the assumed circular path will not occur.
lessons.equation: ΣF_inward = mv²/r
lessons.terms: ΣF_inward: Net inward force component (N). Σ means sum. Outward components enter with a negative sign. m, v, r: Mass, speed and radius (kg, m/s, m). The positive radius is measured to the path centre; m v²/r has units of newtons.

example.title: A horizontal circle model
steps: A 0.5 kg puck moves at 4 m/s on a frictionless horizontal surface, held by a horizontal string of radius 2 m.
Tension supplies the only horizontal inward force.
T = 0.5×16/2 = 4 N. Vertical normal force and weight balance.

visual.title: Centripetal is a role, not an extra force
visual.caption: Tension provides the radial requirement in this specified setup. Do not draw an extra mv²/r interaction arrow.

check.prompt: If the puck speed triples at fixed mass and radius, how does required tension change?
options: It becomes one third as large
It becomes nine times as large
It becomes three times as large
explanations: More speed needs more inward force, not less.
Yes. Required radial force scales with v².
The squared speed gives a factor of nine.

apply.title: Audit a circular-motion diagram
apply.text: A diagram includes tension inward and a second inward arrow labelled “centripetal force.” What is wrong?
apply.answer: It double-counts the same radial role unless a separate physical interaction is identified. Sum actual forces and equate that sum to mv²/r.

lessons.limits: This ideal example ignores string mass, elasticity, maximum load and other real constraints. It is not a safety calculation for rotating equipment.

equationGuide.meaning: Add the actual inward force components and set their total equal to mass times speed squared divided by radius.

symbols.name: Net inward force component
symbols.description: Σ means sum. Outward components enter with a negative sign.

symbols.name: Mass, speed and radius
symbols.description: The positive radius is measured to the path centre; m v²/r has units of newtons.

glossary.definition: Directed toward the centre.
The directed total of the actual forces, not a new separate force.

lessons.title: Separate turning from speeding up
lessons.idea: On a circle, one acceleration component turns the velocity while another changes speed.
body: Keep the circle’s radius fixed and consider an interval without reversal of the rotation direction. Choose the forward tangent to follow the motion. The inward, radial acceleration v²/r turns the velocity. If speed changes too, there is also tangential acceleration.

Tangential acceleration is dv/dt, the rate at which speed changes. It is signed: positive increases speed in the chosen forward direction; negative reduces it. The radial and tangential directions meet at a right angle.

Here ω means angular speed, a nonnegative turning rate. α = dω/dt names its signed rate of change in this no-reversal setup: positive speeds up the turn, negative slows it. At fixed radius r, tangential acceleration is rα. For total acceleration size, square the two perpendicular components, add, then take the square root: √(a_r² + a_t²).
lessons.equation: a_r = v²/r inward;  a_t = dv/dt = rα
lessons.terms: a_r, a_t: Radial magnitude and signed tangential acceleration (m/s²). Radial points inward; tangential is along the path and may speed up or slow down the motion. v, r: Speed and fixed radius (m/s, m). Radius stays constant in this model. ω, α: Angular speed and its time derivative (rad/s, rad/s²). ω is omega; α is alpha. α can be negative when angular speed decreases. dv/dt: Rate of speed change (m/s²). The change in metres per second, per second.

example.title: Turning and accelerating
steps: At an instant, r = 2 m, v = 4 m/s and tangential acceleration is 6 m/s².
Radial acceleration is (4 m/s)² ÷ (2 m) = 8 m/s².
Total acceleration magnitude is √[(8 m/s²)² + (6 m/s²)²] = 10 m/s². The perpendicular contributions combine by the right-triangle rule, not ordinary addition.

visual.title: Separate turning from speeding up
visual.caption: Perpendicular acceleration components combine like perpendicular vector components.

check.prompt: If speed is constant on a circle, which acceleration component is zero?
explanations: Yes. dv/dt = 0, but v²/r can be nonzero.
Changing direction still requires radial acceleration.
Constant speed is not constant velocity on a circle.

apply.title: Connect to a motor
apply.text: In a fixed-radius circular path, what kind of net-force component changes the speed?
apply.answer: A tangential component. A purely radial force is perpendicular to velocity and does no instantaneous work on the ideal point particle.

lessons.limits: If radius changes, the simple fixed-r relations need additional polar-coordinate terms. The present model keeps the path circular with fixed radius. This speed-based description uses a forward direction along the motion and excludes a reversal instant.

practice.prompt: At an instant a cart moves on a fixed-radius 3 m circle at 6 m/s, with tangential acceleration 8 m/s².

parts.label: Total acceleration magnitude
parts.feedback: The perpendicular components combine as √(12²+8²)=√208≈14.4222 m/s².

practice.reasoning: Do not add perpendicular component magnitudes arithmetically. Their directions are part of the acceleration vector.

equationGuide.meaning: The radial part has size speed squared divided by radius. The tangential part is speed’s time derivative, or radius times angular acceleration.

symbols.name: Radial magnitude and signed tangential acceleration
symbols.description: Radial points inward; tangential is along the path and may speed up or slow down the motion.

symbols.name: Speed and fixed radius
symbols.description: Radius stays constant in this model.

symbols.name: Angular speed and its time derivative
symbols.description: ω is omega; α is alpha. α can be negative when angular speed decreases.

symbols.name: Rate of speed change
symbols.description: The change in metres per second, per second.

glossary.definition: Along the tangent to the path.
Here α is the rate of change of angular speed, with forward chosen along the motion and no reversal during the interval. A fixed-axis signed rotation convention is introduced in the rotation module.

lessons.title: Work counts the force along the displacement
lessons.idea: A force transfers mechanical energy through displacement along its direction.
body: Work here means mechanical energy transferred by a force during a displacement. It is not the same as effort or tiredness. For a constant force, only the part along displacement contributes.

A perpendicular force does zero work during that displacement. A force pointing partly opposite the displacement does negative work. The dot product F·Δr calculates this signed along-displacement contribution.

Work has no direction of its own; it is a scalar, a signed number in joules. One joule equals one newton times one metre. For a stationary box, the displacement is zero even if holding it feels tiring.
lessons.equation: W = F·Δr = |F||Δr| cosθ
lessons.terms: W: Work (joules (J)). Energy transferred by this force; positive or negative depending on direction. F, Δr: Force vector and displacement vector (N, m). Δ means change. Bars around either vector mean its size. θ: Angle between force and displacement (degrees or radians consistently). cos θ selects the along-displacement share; · is the dot product, not ordinary vector multiplication.

example.title: Two components
steps: A constant force F = (6,−2) N acts during Δr = (3,1) m.
W = 16 J. The downward component contributes negative work during the upward part.

visual.title: Work counts the force along the displacement
visual.caption: Add the component-by-component work contributions. Work is not the magnitude of a vector.

check.prompt: A 5 N force is perpendicular to a 4 m displacement. What is its work?
explanations: 20 J would require parallel force and displacement.
−20 J would require opposite directions.
Yes. cos90° = 0.

apply.title: Separate effort from mechanical work
apply.text: You hold a box at fixed height without moving it. Is the box’s mechanical work from your upward force positive?
apply.answer: No, the point of application does not move, so that force does zero mechanical work on the stationary box. Your body can still expend metabolic energy; that is a different system and process.

lessons.limits: This particle-work formula must be generalized for extended objects with moving contact points and deformation. Human effort is not identical to mechanical work on the held object.

equationGuide.meaning: Multiply force size by displacement size and by the cosine of their angle. Equivalently, multiply matching components and add them.

symbols.name: Work
symbols.description: Energy transferred by this force; positive or negative depending on direction.

symbols.name: Force vector and displacement vector
symbols.description: Δ means change. Bars around either vector mean its size.

symbols.name: Angle between force and displacement
symbols.description: cos θ selects the along-displacement share; · is the dot product, not ordinary vector multiplication.

glossary.definition: Mechanical energy transferred by force through displacement.
A quantity with a value but no direction.
The energy unit J; one newton-metre.

lessons.title: Integrate a force that changes along the path
lessons.idea: If force changes along a path, add the work from its small pieces.
body: For motion along one axis, a short displacement dx gets work F(x)dx. F(x) means the signed force at position x. Add these pieces from starting position x₁ to ending position x₂ using an integral.
On a force–position graph, that sum is signed area. The horizontal axis is position, not time. Multiplying newtons by metres gives joules, the work unit.

The final force times the whole distance usually gives the wrong work because the force was not always at its final value. A force–time area answers a different question: impulse, taught later, in newton-seconds.
lessons.equation: W = ∫ from x₁ to x₂ F(x) dx
lessons.terms: W: Work (J). The signed energy transfer by the specified force. F(x): Along-axis force at position x (N). May be positive or negative and can vary with position. x₁, x₂: Starting and ending positions (m). Their order specifies the direction of the trip. ∫ … dx: Integral over position (sums N × m to give J). dx identifies position as the variable being added over.

example.title: A growing applied force
steps: Let x name position in metres. A force F(x) = (3 N/m)x increases by 3 newtons for every metre, from x = 0 to x = 2 m.
Force therefore rises linearly from 0 N to 6 N.
The triangular graph area is half its width times height: W = ½ × (2 m) × (6 N) = 6 J of work. This is the same value as the stated integral.

visual.title: Integrate a force that changes along the path
visual.caption: Check the horizontal axis before interpreting an area. The same plotted shape can represent different physical quantities.

check.prompt: For the same F(x), how much work is done from x = 0 to 4 m?
explanations: 48 J uses the final force over the whole distance and doubles the true triangular area.
Yes. ½(3 N/m)(4 m)² = 24 J.
The work grows with the square of the endpoint here.

apply.title: Check a return path
apply.text: If this position-dependent force is traversed backward from x=2 m to 0, what is its work?
apply.answer: −6 J. The signed integration limits reverse, so the same force field contributes the opposite work along the reversed path.

lessons.limits: The expression assumes the specified force depends on position in the stated way. A time-dependent or velocity-dependent force needs the actual trajectory information.

equationGuide.meaning: Add force times each small signed displacement between the two positions to get total work.

symbols.name: Work
symbols.description: The signed energy transfer by the specified force.

symbols.name: Along-axis force at position x
symbols.description: May be positive or negative and can vary with position.

symbols.name: Starting and ending positions
symbols.description: Their order specifies the direction of the trip.

symbols.name: Integral over position
symbols.unit: sums N × m to give J
symbols.description: dx identifies position as the variable being added over.

glossary.definition: The expression being added by an integral.
Force added over time; a later momentum concept, not work.

lessons.title: Net work changes kinetic energy
lessons.idea: Net work tells us how much the energy of motion changes.
body: Kinetic energy means energy of motion. For a constant-mass classical particle, K = ½mv²: half the mass times speed squared. It is nonnegative because mass is positive and a square cannot be negative.
The work–energy theorem says total work from all forces equals final kinetic energy minus initial kinetic energy. “Net” means combine every relevant force’s work, including negative work.

Kinetic energy has no direction sign like velocity. It does depend on the frame, because different moving observers can measure different speeds. The same frame must be used throughout a work–energy calculation.
lessons.equation: K = ½mv²;  W_net = ΔK
lessons.terms: K: Kinetic energy (J). Energy of motion in the chosen inertial frame. m, v: Mass and speed (kg, m/s). Mass is constant; v² means speed multiplied by itself. W_net: Total work of all relevant forces (J). Not necessarily the work of only one applied force. ΔK: Kinetic-energy change (J). Final value minus initial value.

example.title: A speed change
steps: A 2 kg cart changes speed from 1 m/s to 3 m/s.
Initial K = 1 J; final K = 9 J.
Net work = 8 J.

visual.title: Net work changes kinetic energy
visual.caption: A negative velocity can still have positive kinetic energy. Only the speed squared enters K.

check.prompt: At fixed mass, doubling speed changes kinetic energy by what factor?
explanations: Yes. K is proportional to v².
The speed dependence is quadratic, not linear.
Increasing speed increases kinetic energy.

apply.title: Stop with negative work
apply.text: A 1 kg cart moving at 4 m/s is brought to rest. What net work is done?
apply.answer: Initial K = 8 J and final K = 0, so W_net = −8 J. The negative sign means the cart’s kinetic energy decreases.

lessons.limits: The formula is nonrelativistic and assumes constant mass. For extended bodies, include rotational and internal energy where the chosen system requires them.

equationGuide.meaning: Calculate kinetic energy from half mass times speed squared; the final-minus-starting difference equals net work.

symbols.name: Kinetic energy
symbols.description: Energy of motion in the chosen inertial frame.

symbols.name: Mass and speed
symbols.description: Mass is constant; v² means speed multiplied by itself.

symbols.name: Total work of all relevant forces
symbols.description: Not necessarily the work of only one applied force.

symbols.name: Kinetic-energy change
symbols.description: Final value minus initial value.

glossary.definition: The energy associated with motion.
A relationship derived from the stated mathematical and physical assumptions.

lessons.title: Power says how quickly energy is transferred
lessons.idea: Power tells us how quickly work is done, not how much work there is altogether.
body: Average power is work divided by the time taken. The same work done in less time means greater average power. A watt is one joule each second.

Instantaneous means at one moment. For a force on a particle, instantaneous power is F·v. The dot product selects the force component along velocity: same direction adds energy; opposite direction removes it.

Useful mechanical output is not automatically the total energy a machine uses. Other transfers, such as heating, must be counted when assessing efficiency—the fraction of input energy reaching the intended output.
lessons.equation: P_avg = W/Δt;  P = F·v;  1 W = 1 J/s
lessons.terms: P_avg, P: Average and instantaneous power (watts (W)). The rate of mechanical work. W in W/Δt: Work quantity (joules (J)). Here W is a quantity name. After a number, the unit symbol W instead means watts. Δt: Elapsed time (s). A positive interval. F, v: Force and velocity vectors (N, m/s). Their dot product has units N·m/s = J/s.

example.title: A steady lift
steps: A model lift raises a 2 kg mass at 0.4 m/s, using rounded g = 10 m/s².
At constant speed, upward force is 20 N.
Mechanical power delivered to the mass is 20×0.4 = 8 W.

visual.title: Power says how quickly energy is transferred
visual.caption: Same lifting work, shorter time means higher average mechanical power. This is not total electrical input power.

check.prompt: A device does 30 J of useful work in 5 s. What is average useful power?
explanations: Multiplying work by time gives the wrong units.
That divides time by work instead of work by time.

apply.title: Check direction
apply.text: A braking force points opposite velocity. What sign does its instantaneous power have?
apply.answer: Negative. F·v < 0, so that force removes kinetic energy from the particle. The energy is transferred elsewhere rather than destroyed.

lessons.limits: Constant useful output power is not the same as constant force. At P=Fv, the required along-motion force changes with speed.

practice.prompt: An ideal lift raises a 3 kg mass steadily through 2 m in 5 s. Use rounded g=10 m/s² and ignore other losses.

parts.label: Upward force
parts.feedback: Constant speed requires force mg=30 N.

practice.reasoning: This is useful mechanical output, not total electrical input. Real losses would require additional input energy.

equationGuide.meaning: Divide work by elapsed time for average power. At one moment, multiply matching force and velocity components and add. A watt equals a joule per second.

symbols.name: Average and instantaneous power
symbols.description: The rate of mechanical work.

symbols.name: Work quantity
symbols.description: Here W is a quantity name. After a number, the unit symbol W instead means watts.

symbols.name: Elapsed time
symbols.description: A positive interval.

symbols.name: Force and velocity vectors
symbols.description: Their dot product has units N·m/s = J/s.

glossary.definition: Energy transfer per unit time.
One joule per second.
The fraction of input energy or power delivered as the specified useful output.

lessons.title: Store a conservative interaction in a potential
lessons.idea: For a conservative force, work depends on the start and finish, not the route between them.
body: Potential energy U records energy associated with position in a chosen conservative interaction. Conservative means the force’s work between two positions does not depend on the path, within the stated force field and region.

For a time-independent potential in one dimension, force is minus its slope: F(x) = −dU/dx. The derivative dU/dx says how much potential energy changes per small position change. The minus sign makes force point toward decreasing potential energy—not always toward smaller position numbers.

The force’s work equals starting potential energy minus final potential energy. Adding the same constant to every potential-energy value changes neither this difference nor the force. Choosing zero potential energy is a reference choice.
lessons.equation: F(x) = −dU/dx;  W_conservative = U_initial − U_final
lessons.terms: F(x): Force at position x (N). The signed force along the chosen axis. U, U_initial, U_final: Potential energy and endpoint values (J). The zero reference is chosen, but differences have physical consequences. x, dU/dx: Position and potential-energy slope (m, J/m = N). The derivative gives energy change per position change; the minus sign reverses the slope.

example.title: A curved potential
steps: Let U(x) = (3 J/m²)x².
At x = 2 m, F = −12 N. At x = −2 m, F = +12 N: both point toward lower U.

visual.title: Store a conservative interaction in a potential
visual.caption: Potential-energy slope determines force. Potential energy itself is not a force.

check.prompt: If 100 J is added to every potential-energy value, what happens to the force?
explanations: The slope, including its sign, is unchanged.
Yes. The derivative of the added constant is zero.
An energy offset cannot be added to force with different units.

apply.title: Check a closed path
apply.text: What is the net work of a conservative force around a closed path?
apply.answer: Zero, because the initial and final positions have the same potential energy. This test needs the force field and its domain to be appropriately specified.

lessons.limits: Not every force can be represented by a position-only potential. Friction and many velocity-dependent forces need another energy accounting.

equationGuide.meaning: Force is the negative position-slope of potential energy. Work by that force equals the loss of potential energy between the endpoints.

symbols.name: Force at position x

symbols.name: Potential energy and endpoint values

lessons.title: Read allowed motion from E−U
lessons.idea: An energy diagram shows where motion is possible and where speed becomes zero.
body: For one-dimensional conservative motion, total mechanical energy E stays constant. It is kinetic energy plus potential energy. Subtract U(x), the potential energy at a position, from E to get the kinetic energy there.

Kinetic energy cannot be negative in this classical model, so positions need E ≥ U(x). At a turning point the two are equal: speed is zero and the object may reverse direction. The force need not be zero there.

Equilibrium means zero force, which requires zero potential-energy slope dU/dx. Near a smooth upward-curving minimum, a small displacement produces a force back toward the minimum: this equilibrium is stable. Near a downward-curving maximum, the force pushes farther away, so it is unstable. A flat minimum needs more care; zero slope alone does not establish stability.
lessons.equation: ½mv² = E − U(x)
lessons.terms: m, v: Mass and speed (kg, m/s). The left side ½mv² is kinetic energy in joules. E: Conserved mechanical energy (J). Constant for this conservative one-dimensional model. U(x): Potential energy at position x (J). x is position in metres. E − U must be nonnegative for classical motion. v = √[2(E−U)/m]: Speed from available kinetic energy (m/s). Take the nonnegative square root; this gives speed, not the velocity direction.

example.title: A spring-shaped potential
steps: Let U = (2 J/m²)x² and E = 8 J.
Turning points satisfy 2x² = 8 in SI units, giving x = ±2 m.
The equilibrium is x = 0, where U has a minimum and force is zero.

visual.title: Read allowed motion from E−U

check.prompt: At the example’s turning point x = 2 m, must acceleration be zero?
options: No; the restoring force is nonzero there
Yes; zero velocity always means zero acceleration
Yes; all force vanishes when E = U
explanations: Correct. F = −dU/dx = −8 N there, so acceleration is nonzero for finite mass.
Velocity and acceleration are distinct quantities.
E = U sets kinetic energy to zero, not force.

apply.title: Compare two energy levels
apply.text: If E increases in this spring-shaped potential, what happens to the accessible position range?
apply.answer: The turning points move farther from zero because (2 J/m²)x² = E. Higher energy allows a larger oscillation amplitude in this model.

lessons.limits: The diagram assumes one-dimensional conservative classical motion. Dissipation changes E over time; multidimensional accessibility needs more information.

practice.prompt: Use U(x)=(4 J/m²)x², total energy E=16 J, and mass m=2 kg.

lessons.title: Choose an energy zero, then compare changes
lessons.idea: A reference choice shifts potential values without changing the force.
body: A spring stores energy when you stretch or squeeze it. Let x tell us how far it is from its relaxed length: positive for a stretch and negative for a squeeze. The number k tells us how stiff it is. In Uₛ = ½kx², square x, multiply by k, then halve the result. Either sign of a nonzero x gives positive stored energy; x = 0 gives zero.

Raising an object also stores energy in the object–Earth interaction. Near Earth, U_g = mgh: multiply mass, gravity strength and height. You can choose where height and energy count as zero. Moving that zero does not change energy differences or the force. From the earlier slope rule, −dUₛ/dx = −kx and −dU_g/dh = −mg: the spring force points toward its relaxed length x = 0, including outward when squeezed; gravity points downward.
lessons.equation: Uₛ = ½kx²; U_g = mgh
lessons.terms: Uₛ: spring potential energy (J). ½: one half (no unit). k: spring stiffness (N/m). x: signed spring extension (m). U_g: gravitational potential energy (J). m: mass (kg). g: gravity strength (m/s²). h: height (m). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

steps: A spring has k = 120 N/m and x = −0.15 m.
Compression stores positive energy; the positive force points back toward the unstretched position.

Yes. Doubling x multiplies x², and therefore Uₛ, by four.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: A 0.8 kg object rises 0.5 m where g = 9.8 m/s². If you change the height reference by 2 m, does the energy increase change?
apply.answer: The increase stays mgΔh = 0.8 × 9.8 × 0.5 = 3.92 J. Both endpoint potentials shift by the same constant, so their difference is unchanged.

lessons.title: Keep mechanical and total energy separate
lessons.idea: Mechanical energy can decrease while the broader energy account remains balanced.
body: Kinetic energy K is energy of motion. Potential energy U records stored energy, such as spring or height energy. Their sum K + U is called mechanical energy. Other forces can add to this sum or take away from it. Call their work W_nc. The rule Δ(K + U) = W_nc says that the change in mechanical energy equals this extra work.

For example, a block sliding across a fixed rough floor loses mechanical energy through friction. If we also count the floor, that energy goes into other forms, including heating and small changes of shape. Total energy has not vanished. Always say which objects and which kinds of energy you are counting.
lessons.equation: Δ(K + U) = W_nc
lessons.terms: Δ: change (no unit). K: kinetic energy (J). U: potential energy (J). W_nc: other work (J). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: A block begins with K = 8 J on a level surface, so U does not change.
Friction does W_nc = −3 J over the chosen displacement.
The final kinetic energy is 8 − 3 = 5 J. The broader account has a corresponding 3 J internal-energy increase under the stated assumptions.

check.prompt: A system starts with K + U = 9 J. A nonconservative external drive adds 4 J and friction removes 2 J. What is its final mechanical energy?
explanations: This subtracts both transfers; the drive adds energy.
This adds the friction transfer instead of subtracting it.
Yes. The net work is +4 − 2 = +2 J, giving 11 J.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: A block loses 2 J of kinetic energy while climbing and gains 2 J of potential energy. Does that alone prove friction acted?
apply.answer: No. Δ(K + U) = −2 + 2 = 0 J. This is consistent with purely conservative conversion, though equal positive and negative nonconservative transfers could also cancel.

lessons.limits: This is a mechanical-energy model with clearly chosen interactions. An energy balance alone does not identify every force or establish the temperature change without thermal information.

practice.prompt: On a level track, a block starts with 12 J of kinetic energy. Constant sliding friction of magnitude 2 N opposes a 3 m displacement. No other horizontal force does work. Find friction work and final kinetic energy.
practice.reasoning: The block still has positive kinetic energy after the stated travel, consistent with continued sliding. Numerical tolerance is 10⁻⁸ in each stated unit, allowing rounding of these exact small-number calculations.

lessons.title: Keep the direction in momentum
lessons.idea: Momentum is mass times velocity, so opposite velocities produce opposite momenta.
body: Momentum p combines mass and velocity: p = mv. Velocity includes direction, so momentum does too. On a line, a plus or minus sign tells us the direction. With x and y directions, multiply each velocity part by mass separately.

Momentum is not the same as kinetic energy. Motion energy uses speed squared, K = ½mv², so changing direction alone does not change it. Two equal objects moving equally fast in opposite directions have momenta that cancel. Their motion energies still add: the objects are moving even though total momentum is zero.
lessons.equation: p = mv; pₓ = mvₓ; pᵧ = mvᵧ
lessons.terms: p: momentum (kg·m/s). m: mass (kg). v: velocity (m/s). pₓ, pᵧ: momentum components (kg·m/s). vₓ, vᵧ: velocity components (m/s). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

lessons.title: Accumulate force over time
lessons.idea: Impulse is the area under a force–time graph and equals momentum change.
body: A force changes momentum while it acts. Impulse J adds up that force over time. If the force changes, add the areas under its force–time graph; the integral sign ∫ means this continuous adding. Work with one direction at a time and subtract areas below zero. A triangular pulse above zero has area ½ × duration × peak force.

Average force means impulse divided by the time taken. The same impulse spread over more time gives a smaller average force. But average and peak are different: peak is the largest force reached. Two pulses can have the same area and different peaks.
lessons.equation: J = ∫F_net dt = p_final − p_initial; F_avg = J/Δt
lessons.terms: J: impulse (N·s or kg·m/s). ∫: integral (no unit by itself). F_net: net force (N). dt: tiny time interval (s). p_final, p_initial: final and initial momentum (kg·m/s). F_avg: average force (N). Δt: elapsed time (s). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

lessons.title: Choose a system before conserving momentum
lessons.idea: A system conserves total momentum when its net external impulse is zero.
body: Choose which objects belong to your system, then add all their momenta to get total momentum P. Forces between those objects come in equal opposite pairs. Their impulses cancel in the total. Forces from outside the system do not automatically cancel.

Total momentum stays the same if the combined outside impulse is zero. It stays nearly the same if that impulse is small enough to ignore for your question. The outside forces do not each have to be zero. For example, their total effect during a very short contact may be small. Always check the system boundary and time interval first.
lessons.equation: P = Σpᵢ; P_final − P_initial = J_external
lessons.terms: P: total momentum (kg·m/s). Σ: sum sign (no unit by itself). pᵢ: momentum of body i (kg·m/s). P_final, P_initial: final and initial totals (kg·m/s). J_external: outside impulse (N·s). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Two initially stationary carts, masses 0.3 kg and 0.9 kg, push apart using an internal spring. External horizontal impulse is negligible.
If the lighter cart ends at +1.8 m/s, then 0.3 × 1.8 + 0.9v = 0.
The heavier cart has v = −0.6 m/s. The equal opposite momenta need not mean equal speeds.

lessons.title: Track the mass-weighted position
lessons.idea: The centre of mass responds to total external force, not internal rearrangement alone.
body: The centre of mass is an average position that gives more weight to heavier objects. Multiply each position by its mass, add the results, then divide by total mass. The answer lies closer to the heavier object. It can even be in an empty gap between objects.

The same kind of average gives the centre-of-mass velocity. Total momentum divided by total mass gives this velocity. Outside force determines how the centre of mass accelerates. The objects can move around each other, but their internal pushes alone cannot accelerate their shared centre of mass.

P: total momentum (kg·m/s). a_CM: centre-of-mass acceleration (m/s²). F_external: combined outside force (N). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. lessons.title: Check kinetic energy as well as momentum
lessons.idea: Momentum conservation does not by itself make a collision elastic.
body: During a collision, use momentum conservation only when the outside impulse is small enough to ignore. Then separately check kinetic energy, the energy of motion. An elastic collision keeps the same total kinetic energy. An inelastic collision changes some of it into other forms. Perfectly inelastic means the bodies stick and move together afterward.

Bouncing does not by itself mean elastic: bodies can separate and still lose kinetic energy. In the ordinary collisions here, lost motion energy goes into heating, sound or changes of shape. It is not destroyed. A spring release could instead add motion energy, so always examine the energy account as well as the momentum account.
lessons.equation: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v  (if the bodies stick)
lessons.terms: m₁, m₂: body masses (kg). u₁, u₂: initial velocities (m/s). v: shared final velocity (m/s). m₁ + m₂: combined mass (kg). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: A 0.8 kg cart at +3 m/s sticks to a stationary 0.4 kg cart.
Initial momentum is +2.4 kg·m/s, so the combined velocity is 2.4/1.2 = +2 m/s.
Initial K = 3.6 J and final K = 2.4 J. The 1.2 J decrease is mechanical-energy transfer, not disappearance of total energy.

apply.answer: No. Internal stored energy can be released, such as by a spring. That is outside the passive-loss classification used in the example; momentum and kinetic energy are separate checks.

lessons.title: Solve momentum and energy together
lessons.idea: An elastic collision supplies two conservation equations, not a guessed exchange rule.
body: For an elastic collision along one line, conserve both momentum and kinetic energy. Consider two equal masses, with one initially at rest. After dividing out the common mass, the momentum rule says u = v₁ + v₂. The energy rule says u² = v₁² + v₂². Here u is the approaching body’s initial velocity and v₁, v₂ are the final velocities.

Square the momentum rule: u² = v₁² + 2v₁v₂ + v₂². Comparing the two rules gives v₁v₂ = 0, so at least one final velocity is zero. The solution with v₂ = 0 leaves everything unchanged. For a completed impact where the approaching bodies separate, use the other solution: v₁ = 0 and v₂ = u. This result depends on equal masses and a target initially at rest.
lessons.equation: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂; ½m₁u₁² + ½m₂u₂² = ½m₁v₁² + ½m₂v₂²
lessons.terms: m₁, m₂: body masses (kg). u₁, u₂: velocities before impact (m/s). v₁, v₂: velocities after impact (m/s). ½mu², ½mv²: kinetic-energy terms (J). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Two 0.7 kg carts collide elastically along a line. The approaching first cart moves at +2.4 m/s; the second starts at rest.
The separating solution has v₁ = 0 and v₂ = +2.4 m/s.
Momentum is +1.68 kg·m/s on each side, and kinetic energy is ½ × 0.7 × 2.4² = 2.016 J on each side.

apply.answer: No. Momentum would change from +2 to +6 kg·m/s. Equal-mass velocity transfer cannot be carried over to unequal masses; solve the two conservation equations with the actual masses.

lessons.title: Balance each momentum component
lessons.idea: Two-dimensional conservation requires both x and y momentum balances.
body: Momentum has direction. In a two-direction collision, choose perpendicular x and y directions. Add the x momenta before contact and match their total afterward. Do the same for y. Getting one direction right is not enough.

If the bodies stick, divide each total momentum component by the combined mass to find that part of their shared velocity. If the bodies separate, you may have more unknown velocities than equations. Then you need more information, such as one outgoing direction or a statement that the collision is elastic.
lessons.equation: Pₓ = Σmᵢvₓᵢ; Pᵧ = Σmᵢvᵧᵢ; vₓ,final = Pₓ/M; vᵧ,final = Pᵧ/M  (sticking)

M: combined mass (kg). vₓ,final, vᵧ,final: shared final velocity components (m/s). Final velocity is (+1, +1.5) m/s. It is not found by adding the two initial speeds.

lessons.title: Describe turning with angular rates
lessons.idea: Angular position, velocity and acceleration play different roles, just as linear ones do.
body: Choose the line a wheel turns around and choose which turning direction is positive. Angle θ tells you its orientation. Angular velocity ω tells you how fast that angle changes, including direction. Angular acceleration α tells you how fast ω changes. Use radians for angle: one full turn is 2π radians.

If angular acceleration stays constant, use the same pattern as the earlier straight-line motion rules. Add αt to the starting angular velocity. The angle turned is ω₀t + ½αt². Every point on a rigid wheel shares the same turning rate, but a point farther from the axis travels farther each turn and has a greater speed.
lessons.equation: ω = ω₀ + αt; Δθ = ω₀t + ½αt²; speed = r|ω|
lessons.terms: ω, ω₀: final and starting angular velocity (rad/s). α: angular acceleration (rad/s²). t: elapsed time (s). Δθ: angle turned (rad). ½αt²: extra angle from acceleration (rad). r: distance from the rotation axis (m). |ω|: angular-speed magnitude (rad/s). speed: point speed (m/s). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: A wheel starts at ω₀ = +1 rad/s with constant α = +0.5 rad/s².
After 4 s, ω = 1 + 0.5 × 4 = +3 rad/s and Δθ = 1 × 4 + ½ × 0.5 × 16 = 8 rad.
A point 0.2 m from the axis then has speed 0.2 × 3 = 0.6 m/s.

lessons.title: Weight each mass by distance squared
lessons.idea: Moment of inertia depends on how mass is spread relative to a chosen axis.
body: Mass farther from the rotation axis moves faster for the same turning rate. To count its effect, multiply each small mass by the square of its shortest distance from the axis, then add. This total is the moment of inertia I. It describes how mass is spread around that particular axis.

For a solid body, imagine many tiny pieces of mass. The integral ∫r_perp² dm adds their contributions continuously instead of listing every piece. The energy of rigid turning about a fixed axis is K_rot = ½Iω². Moving mass outward increases I even if total mass stays the same.
lessons.equation: I = Σmᵢr_perp,i² = ∫r_perp² dm; K_rot = ½Iω²
lessons.terms: I: moment of inertia (kg·m²). Σ: sum sign (no unit by itself). mᵢ: mass of piece i (kg). r_perp,i: perpendicular distance of piece i (m). ∫: integral (no unit by itself). dm: tiny mass piece (kg). r_perp: perpendicular distance (m). K_rot: rotational kinetic energy (J). ω: angular velocity (rad/s). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

steps: Three small attached masses rotate about an axis: 0.2 kg at radius 0.1 m, 0.3 kg at 0.2 m, and 0.5 kg directly on the axis. Neglect the support mass.
At ω = 5 rad/s, K_rot = ½ × 0.014 × 25 = 0.175 J. The on-axis point mass contributes no rotational kinetic energy.

lessons.title: Shift an axis without changing its direction
lessons.idea: A parallel axis away from the centre of mass adds Md² to the moment of inertia.
body: Suppose you know an object’s moment of inertia about a line through its centre of mass. What if it turns about another line pointing the same way? These are parallel axes. The new moment of inertia is the old value plus Md², where M is total mass and d is the shortest distance between the two lines.

The starting axis must pass through the centre of mass. The new axis must be parallel to it. The added Md² cannot be negative, so moving away from that centre axis increases the moment of inertia. This rule does not apply just because you know the distance between any two axes.
lessons.equation: I = I_CM + Md²
lessons.terms: I: shifted-axis moment of inertia (kg·m²). I_CM: centre-axis moment of inertia (kg·m²). M: total mass (kg). d: axis separation (m). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: A rigid object of mass 2 kg has measured I_CM = 0.04 kg·m² about a specified centre axis.
Shift to a parallel axis 0.3 m away: I = 0.04 + 2 × 0.3².
The result is 0.22 kg·m². Shifting the axis increases I without changing the object’s mass.

lessons.title: Count translation and rotation together
lessons.idea: A rolling body carries both centre-of-mass motion and rotation about its centre.
body: A wheel can move forward while also turning. If it rolls without sliding on a stationary floor, its centre speed is angular speed times radius: v_CM = |ω|R. The point touching the floor is briefly at rest relative to the floor. A spinning wheel that slides does not obey this no-slip rule.

Count both kinds of motion energy: energy from the centre moving, plus energy from turning around the centre. Use I_CM, the moment of inertia about the centre, for the turning part. In ideal rolling, static friction can help maintain rolling without slipping, without removing energy: the touching point is not moving. Real sliding or changes of shape can still turn motion energy into heat.
lessons.equation: v_CM = |ω|R; K = ½Mv_CM² + ½I_CMω²
lessons.terms: v_CM: centre-of-mass speed (m/s). |ω|: angular-speed magnitude (rad/s). R: rolling radius (m). K: total kinetic energy (J). M: total mass (kg). I_CM: centre-axis moment of inertia (kg·m²). ½Mv_CM²: energy of centre motion (J). ½I_CMω²: energy of turning about the centre (J). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (a force unit), J joule (an energy unit), and rad radian (an angle unit). A dot multiplies units; / means per. Squared, ², means multiplied by itself. For example, m/s² describes velocity change in metres per second each second.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: A rigid wheel has M = 2 kg, R = 0.2 m and I_CM = 0.04 kg·m². It rolls without slipping at v_CM = 1 m/s.
Its angular-speed magnitude is 1/0.2 = 5 rad/s. Translational K is ½ × 2 × 1² = 1 J.
Rotational K is ½ × 0.04 × 5² = 0.5 J, so total K = 1.5 J.

lessons.title: Measure a force’s turning effect
lessons.idea: Torque combines a force with its position relative to a chosen origin.
body: A force can push an object and can also turn it. Torque is the turning effect about a chosen point, called the origin O. A vector records both size and direction. The position vector r goes from O to where the force F acts. The cross product r × F combines these vectors to give the torque vector τ (tau). Its size is force times the perpendicular distance from O to the force’s line. That distance is the lever arm d.

If θ (theta) is the angle between r and F, the lever arm is r sin θ: sin is the sine function that picks out the perpendicular part. Curl your right-hand fingers from r toward F; your thumb gives the torque direction. On our page, x is right, y is up and +z is out toward you. A force aimed along a line through O has no turning effect about O. Changing O can change the torque. Torque and work can both use N·m, but torque has direction and work is an energy transfer.
lessons.equation: τ = r × F; |τ| = rF sin θ = Fd
lessons.terms: τ: torque (N·m); Turning effect about O; τz is its signed part along z. r: position vector or its size (m); From O to the force application point; r without a vector direction in the size formula is its length. F: force vector or its size (N); The push or pull; F in the size formula is its size. θ: angle (rad); Angle between position and force; sin θ gives the perpendicular fraction. d: lever arm (m); Shortest distance from O to the line along which the force acts. O: origin (none); Chosen point about which torque is measured. |τ|: torque magnitude (N·m); Vertical bars ask for the size, without its direction. Unit key: m = metre, s = second, kg = kilogram, N = newton (kg·m/s²), J = joule (N·m), rad = radian (angle); MJ = one million joules. A dot joins multiplied units; / means per; ² means squared and ³ means cubed. Thus rad/s is radians per second and rad/s² is the change in rad/s each second.

example.title: Calculate a signed torque
steps: Take r = (0.40,0,0) m and F = (0,15,0) N. The force is perpendicular to r.
τz = (0.40 m)(15 N) = +6.0 N·m. The positive sign means out of the page.
The other components vanish; this calculation does not say the body is already rotating.

check.prompt: Keep r = (0.40,0,0) m but use F = (0,−5,0) N. What is τz?
explanations: The magnitude is 2.0, but reversing the force reverses the torque direction.
Multiply 0.40 by −5: the signed z component is −2.0 N·m.
The force remains perpendicular to r, so its lever arm is not zero.

apply.title: Try the idea in another case
apply.text: Can a large force have zero torque about a chosen origin?
apply.answer: Yes. If its line of action passes through that origin, d = 0. A zero torque about that point does not mean the force is absent.

lessons.limits: Use a common origin for all torques being added. This is classical mechanics; no material-strength or tool-use safety conclusion follows.

lessons.title: Use net torque to predict angular acceleration
lessons.idea: For a fixed-axis rigid body, net axial torque changes angular velocity rather than setting it directly.
body: An axis is a line around which an object turns. Here the axis stays fixed and the object is rigid: its shape does not change. Moment of inertia I measures how hard it is to change its spin about that axis. Angular velocity ω (omega) describes the rate and direction of turning. Angular acceleration α (alpha) describes how quickly that rate changes. Add all outside turning effects along the axis, with their signs, to get net torque τnet. Divide this total by I to find α.

Choose one turning direction as positive. A positive torque gives positive angular acceleration, but it can slow an object already turning in the negative direction. Zero total torque means the spin rate stays the same, not necessarily that it stops. Include resistance from the supports, such as friction. The simple equation here requires I to stay constant.
lessons.equation: τnet = Iα; for constant α, ωf = ωi + αΔt
lessons.terms: τnet: net axial torque (N·m); Signed total of all outside turning effects along the fixed axis. I: moment of inertia (kg·m²); Resistance to changing spin about the chosen axis. α: angular acceleration (rad/s²); Change in angular velocity each second. ωi, ωf: initial and final angular velocity (rad/s); Signed turning rate before and after the interval. Δt: elapsed time (s); Final time minus initial time; Δ means change. lessons.title: Balance both forces and torques
lessons.idea: An object at rest remains in static equilibrium only when both external force and torque balance.
body: Static equilibrium means an object stays at rest. For a rigid object, whose shape stays the same, two balances are needed: the forces must add to zero and the turning effects must add to zero. We judge rest in a nonaccelerating frame of reference. The centre of mass is the point that tracks the object’s overall motion. Balanced forces prevent its acceleration, but forces can still turn the object unless torques balance too. Σ means add the listed quantities, including their directions and signs.

Choose a point about which to add torques. A force applied at that point has no lever arm and contributes no torque about it. This can remove an unknown from one equation. It does not create a physical support. In our bar example, each support pushes upward on the bar; this push is called a support reaction. First find one support force from torque balance, then find the other from force balance.

steps: Use a weightless horizontal rigid bar 3.0 m long, supported at both ends. A downward 18 N point load acts 1.0 m from the left end.

Vertical force balance gives RL + 6 − 18 = 0, so RL = 12 N. Both balances hold.

The load’s torque arm changed; the old reactions no longer balance torque.

apply.answer: Yes. If their lines of action are separated, they can have zero net force but a nonzero net torque. The body can begin turning.

lessons.title: Attach angular momentum to an origin
lessons.idea: A moving particle can have angular momentum about a point even without moving in a circle.
body: Linear momentum p is mass m times velocity v. Angular momentum L describes motion about a chosen point, including a direction. It is not limited to spinning objects: a particle moving in a straight line can have angular momentum about a point away from that line. Let r point from the chosen origin to the particle. The cross product r × p gives L, with the same right-hand direction rule used for torque. If r and p lie along the same line, the result is zero.

For an object whose shape stays fixed and which turns about a fixed axis, the part of angular momentum along that axis equals moment of inertia times angular velocity. The subscript “axis” means we select this part. Do not assume the whole angular-momentum vector always points along the rotation axis. They line up for certain special axes, called principal axes; finding those axes for an arbitrary body is beyond this lesson.

steps: At one instant, a 0.50 kg particle is at r = (2,0,0) m and moves with v = (0,3,0) m/s.
Its momentum is p = (0,1.5,0) kg·m/s.
Therefore Lz = 2×1.5 = 3.0 kg·m²/s. A circular trajectory was not required.

lessons.title: Check the external torque before conserving L
lessons.idea: Total angular momentum stays constant when net external torque about the chosen fixed inertial origin vanishes.
body: Choose which objects belong to the system. Also choose an origin that stays fixed in a nonaccelerating and nonrotating frame. An external torque is a turning effect caused by something outside that system. The equation dL/dt = τext says that the total angular momentum changes at a rate equal to the total external torque. If this torque is zero, total angular momentum stays unchanged. Parts inside the system can exchange angular momentum without changing the total.

A force directed straight toward or away from the origin has zero torque about it, because its lever arm is zero. Such a force is called central. Even a small nonzero torque can add up over time. When its component along the chosen axis stays constant, multiply that torque by the elapsed time to get the change in angular momentum along the axis. This accumulated turning effect is called angular impulse.

lessons.title: Separate conserved rotation from changing energy
lessons.idea: A decrease in inertia can raise spin speed while conserving angular momentum, but not rotational kinetic energy.
body: Suppose a rotating system has no total outside turning effect along its fixed axis. Its parts move closer to or farther from that axis in a balanced way. Compare the state before this movement with the state after it: in both states the parts share one angular velocity. Angular momentum stays the same, so initial inertia times initial angular velocity equals the final product. The object can change shape during the movement.

At these two end states, assume no parts are still moving toward or away from the axis relative to their shared rotation. Their rotational kinetic energy—the energy of spinning—is one half times inertia times angular velocity squared. It also equals angular momentum squared divided by twice the inertia. At the same nonzero angular momentum, smaller inertia means more spinning energy. Work done inside the system supplies that increase from another energy store; it is not free energy. Include heat or other internal motion if present.

steps: Let Ii = 0.80 kg·m², ωi = 3.0 rad/s and If = 0.40 kg·m².

Zero external torque conserves angular momentum; it does not independently conserve rotational kinetic energy.

apply.text: Why is τ = Iα alone insufficient while I is changing?
apply.answer: While I changes, the product Iω can change in two ways: the angular velocity ω changes, or the inertia I changes. The product rule gives τext,axis = Iα + ω(dI/dt). Here α is angular acceleration in rad/s², dI/dt is inertia change per second in kg·m²/s, and τext,axis is external axial torque in N·m. Ignoring the second contribution would wrongly predict no spin change when torque is zero.

lessons.title: Measure separation from the mass centre
lessons.idea: Outside a spherical source, Newtonian gravitational force decreases with the square of centre distance.
body: Newton’s gravity law gives the attractive force between two point masses: objects treated as having all their mass at one point. Multiply their masses M and m by the gravitational constant G, then divide by the square of their separation r. The force points along the line joining them. Outside a spherical source whose mass is distributed the same way in every direction from its centre, the same rule works using the source’s centre. Distance here is not height above the surface.

Divide force by the small object’s mass m to get its gravitational acceleration g. We write μ (mu) for G times the source mass M, just to shorten the calculation. Doubling m doubles force, but not the acceleration. Squaring distance means multiplying distance by itself, so doubling the distance divides force by four. These are classical gravity rules, not the strong-gravity description needed near objects such as black holes.

lessons.title: Set an energy threshold for escape
lessons.idea: With zero potential at infinity, the escape threshold is total mechanical energy zero.
body: Potential energy is energy associated with position in a force field. Choose gravitational potential energy U to be zero at infinitely large separation: a reference approached as distance keeps growing without bound. Outside our fixed spherical source, U is minus μ times the small mass m divided by centre distance r. Moving farther away raises U toward zero. Its negative value reflects the chosen reference, not a negative speed. Shifting every potential energy by the same constant leaves the force unchanged.

The ideal escape threshold is the lowest starting speed that allows the object to travel arbitrarily far away, with speed tending to zero, without further driving or resistance. At this threshold, positive kinetic energy exactly balances negative potential energy. Solving that balance gives the square root of 2μ/r. A direction leading into the source is still excluded. This calculation does not tell us rocket fuel needs, steering or real launch performance.

lessons.title: Let gravity bend an orbit continuously
lessons.idea: A circular orbit is free fall with a speed that produces the required centripetal acceleration.
body: To move in a circle, an object needs acceleration toward the centre even when its speed stays the same. Its size is speed squared divided by radius. This is called centripetal acceleration. In a circular orbit powered only by gravity, gravity must supply exactly this acceleration. Equating the required force to gravity and dividing out the small object’s mass gives circular speed √(μ/r). The object is falling freely: gravity keeps changing the direction of its motion.

The period T is the time for one whole trip. A circle has length 2πr, so divide that length by the circular speed to get T. Equivalently, T is 2π times the square root of radius cubed divided by μ; cubed means r times r times r. These speed and period formulas describe circular paths. A different speed or direction at the same position generally produces a different path, which may hit the source.

T: orbital period (s); Time for one full orbit. π: pi (none); Circumference divided by diameter, about 3.14159. m, M: orbiting and central masses (kg); M≫m means the central mass is much larger. vesc: escape threshold speed (m/s); At the same radius it is √2 times circular speed. lessons.title: Use the sign and size of orbital energy
lessons.idea: A circular gravitational orbit has negative total energy when potential is zero at infinity.
body: Kinetic energy K is energy of motion; potential energy U here is energy associated with position in gravity. Total mechanical energy E is their sum. For a circular orbit, insert the circular-speed formula into K=½mv². This gives K=μm/(2r), while U=−μm/r. The negative potential energy has twice the size of the positive kinetic energy. Their sum is negative: E=−μm/(2r). A different circular radius has a different total energy.

For an isolated orbit shaped like an ellipse, the same energy formula uses a, the semimajor axis: half of the ellipse’s longest diameter. The distance from the source at a particular moment is usually not a. The source lies at one focus, a special point inside the ellipse, not at the ellipse’s centre. A negative energy means a bound orbit: the object cannot get arbitrarily far away under this model alone. At zero or positive energy it is not gravitationally bound. These statements use potential energy set to zero at infinity and exclude collisions with the source.
lessons.equation: Ecircular = −μm/(2 r); Eellipse = −μm/(2 a)
lessons.terms: Ecircular, Eellipse: total mechanical energy (J); Subscripts label the circular or elliptical path; E=K+U. K, U: kinetic and potential energy (J); Energy of motion and gravity-position energy. μ: source gravitational parameter (m³/s²); G times central mass M. m, M: orbiting and source masses (kg); M is assumed much larger than m. r: circular radius (m); Fixed centre distance on a circular orbit. a: semimajor axis (m); Half the longest diameter of the ellipse. v: orbital speed (m/s); Size of the object’s velocity. Unit key: m = metre, s = second, kg = kilogram, N = newton (kg·m/s²), J = joule (N·m), rad = radian (angle); MJ = one million joules. A dot joins multiplied units; / means per; ² means squared and ³ means cubed. Thus rad/s is radians per second and rad/s² is the change in rad/s each second.

steps: For μ=8.0×10¹² m³/s², m=3.0 kg and circular radius r=2.0×10⁶ m, v=2000 m/s.
E=−6.0×10⁶ J. A circular orbit at twice the radius has E=−3.0×10⁶ J: it needs a net energy increase, despite its lower final speed.

apply.title: Try the idea in another case
apply.text: Why is one orbit’s energy insufficient to determine its complete shape?
apply.answer: Different angular momenta can give different eccentricities (different degrees of orbital elongation) at the same negative energy. Energy fixes a in this model, but additional position/velocity information is needed.

lessons.limits: The energy-sign classification assumes infinity-zero potential and isolated Newtonian point-mass motion with M≫m. Radial collision trajectories and source surfaces require extra care; negative energy is not a collision-safety guarantee.

lessons.title: Choose a balance law from the conditions
lessons.idea: The requested unknown and the stated interactions determine which balance law is useful.
body: Choose the objects in your system and the time interval first. To find acceleration or a contact force, draw the chosen object with arrows for the forces on it: a free-body diagram. Then add forces and use mass times acceleration. To link speeds at two positions, an energy account may avoid calculating every moment between them. During a brief collision, momentum can connect before and after if outside forces give no appreciable total impulse. Impulse is force accumulated over time.

These are compatible ways to describe the same motion. They work only with the right conditions. An outside impulse changes system momentum. A sticking collision can conserve total momentum while converting kinetic energy into heating or deformation. Conserved means unchanged over the chosen interval; do not assume a quantity is conserved just because that makes the calculation easier.
lessons.equation: ΣF = ma; Δ(K+U) = Wnonconservative; Δp = Jexternal
lessons.terms: ΣF: net force (N); Sum of forces with their directions. m, a: mass and acceleration (kg; m/s²); Mass of the selected object and rate its velocity changes. Δ: change (none); Final value minus initial value. K, U: kinetic and potential energy (J); Energy of motion and energy associated with position. Wnonconservative: work not represented by potential energy (J); Energy transferred by the remaining forces in the chosen account. p: momentum (kg·m/s); Mass times velocity. Jexternal: external impulse (kg·m/s); Outside force accumulated over time; this variable J is not the unit J meaning joule. Unit key: m = metre, s = second, kg = kilogram, N = newton (kg·m/s²), J = joule (N·m), rad = radian (angle); MJ = one million joules. A dot joins multiplied units; / means per; ² means squared and ³ means cubed. Thus rad/s is radians per second and rad/s² is the change in rad/s each second.

example.title: A collision selects momentum
steps: A 0.40 kg cart at 3.0 m/s catches a stationary 0.20 kg cart and sticks on a horizontal track. External horizontal impulse during contact is negligible.
Initial momentum is 1.2 kg·m/s, so common speed is 1.2/0.60=2.0 m/s.
Kinetic energy changes from 1.8 J to 1.2 J. The 0.6 J difference becomes other forms; conserving mechanical kinetic energy here would give a wrong answer.

options: Equating initial and final system momentum without including the impulse.
Using any form of Newton’s laws.
explanations: Energy bookkeeping remains valid when transfers and other forms are included.
Use pf−pi=Jexternal rather than setting that change to zero.

apply.title: Try the idea in another case
apply.text: An object slides down a smooth fixed ramp. You want only its final speed, not travel time. Which approach is economical?
apply.answer: For the object–Earth system, use the loss of gravitational potential energy and gain in kinetic energy, provided the normal force does no work and losses are negligible. For the normal contact force, a force equation would be needed instead.

lessons.limits: Choosing a useful equation does not remove assumptions. Work/impulse of external interactions must be included over the actual interval, and all components must use consistent signs.

equationGuide.meaning: Total force equals mass times acceleration. Change in kinetic plus potential energy equals work by forces not represented in that potential energy. Momentum change equals outside impulse.

lessons.title: Connect a drive, a collision and a spring
lessons.idea: A multistage event can require a different balance law in each stage.
body: Split this cart story into three intervals: a steady push speeds up one cart, it hits and sticks to another cart, then both compress a spring. The horizontal track has no friction and we ignore wheel rotation. The push stops before the collision. Neither cart touches the spring until after the sticking is complete, so the spring cannot change the collision momentum.

During the push, use force divided by mass to find acceleration. During sticking, conserve the total momentum of both carts; some kinetic energy becomes heating and deformation. After sticking, conserve the kinetic energy of the carts plus the spring’s stored energy. A linear spring stores ½kx². Its stiffness k tells how much extra force is needed per metre of compression. At maximum compression the carts momentarily stop, so their post-collision kinetic energy is all stored in the ideal spring.
lessons.equation: a = F/m; v = at; V = mv/(m+M); ½(m+M)V² = ½kx²
lessons.terms: F: driving force (N); Constant push on the incoming cart before collision. m, M: incoming and waiting cart masses (kg); m is pushed first; M waits at rest. a: incoming cart acceleration (m/s²); Change in its velocity per second during the push. t: push duration (s); Time over which the driving force acts. v: incoming speed (m/s); Speed just before sticking. V: shared speed (m/s); Speed of both carts just after sticking; capital V differs from v. k: spring stiffness (N/m); Force per metre of compression in the ideal linear spring. x: maximum spring compression (m); How far the spring is shortened when the carts momentarily stop. Unit key: m = metre, s = second, kg = kilogram, N = newton (kg·m/s²), J = joule (N·m), rad = radian (angle); MJ = one million joules. A dot joins multiplied units; / means per; ² means squared and ³ means cubed. Thus rad/s is radians per second and rad/s² is the change in rad/s each second.

example.title: Follow one invented sequence
steps: Drive a 0.50 kg cart from rest with 1.0 N for 2.0 s. a=2.0 m/s² and v=4.0 m/s.
It sticks to a stationary 1.5 kg cart. Momentum 2.0 kg·m/s gives V=1.0 m/s for the combined 2.0 kg.
Their post-collision kinetic energy is 1.0 J. On reaching an uncompressed 50 N/m spring, maximum compression satisfies 25 x²=1.0, so x=0.20 m.
The original moving cart had 4.0 J just before contact; 3.0 J became nonmechanical forms during sticking. The spring stores only the remaining 1.0 J.

check.prompt: If only spring stiffness is multiplied by four, how does maximum compression change?
explanations: A stiffer spring stores the same energy at a smaller compression.
With energy fixed, x=√(2 K/k); a factor 4 in k gives a factor½ in x.
Compression is proportional to 1/√k for a fixed incoming energy.

apply.title: Try the idea in another case
apply.text: Why can the collision and compression not be treated as one interval conserving only kinetic plus spring energy?
apply.answer: The sticking collision converts some initial kinetic energy to deformation and thermal/internal energy. Ignoring that conversion would overpredict spring compression.

lessons.limits: Assume negligible external horizontal collision impulse, no rebound, an ideal linear spring within its model range and no losses after sticking. This hypothetical exercise is not a device or impact-safety design.

practice.prompt: Fresh sequence: a 0.60 kg cart starts from rest under 1.2 N for 1.5 s. The drive stops. It sticks to a stationary 0.90 kg cart, then the pair compresses an initially uncompressed 54 N/m spring. The same ideal interval assumptions apply.

parts.label: Kinetic energy converted during collision
parts.feedback: Before:½×0.60×3²=2.70 J. After:1.08 J. Difference 1.62 J.

practice.reasoning: Identify each system and interval before calculating. If the target cart mass tends to zero, the collision speed tends to the incoming speed and its kinetic-energy loss tends to zero. Exact-number tolerances are arithmetic checks.

equationGuide.meaning: Find acceleration from force divided by mass, then speed from acceleration times time from rest. Divide incoming momentum by total mass to get the shared speed. Finally equate shared kinetic energy to stored spring energy.

lessons.title: Test a new rotating system
lessons.idea: A clean assessment changes the physical conditions, not just the labels on a familiar calculation.
body: An ideal rotor turns about one fixed line. First, an outside turning effect acts steadily while the rotor keeps the same shape. Then that turning effect is removed and an internal mechanism moves parts inward in a balanced way. Compare the start and end of this rearrangement, when no parts are still moving toward or away from the axis relative to their shared turning. These are two different intervals, with different conditions.

In the first interval, divide torque by inertia to find how quickly angular velocity changes, then multiply by time to find its increase. In the second, no outside axial torque acts, so inertia times angular velocity stays constant. Compare rotational kinetic energy, ½Iω², before and after the rearrangement; internal work can change that energy. Explain why angular momentum changes during the drive but stays constant during the ideal rearrangement.
lessons.equation: Driven: α = τnet/I. Torque-free rearrangement: Iiωi = Ifωf. Endpoint Krot = ½Iω².
lessons.terms: α: angular acceleration (rad/s²); Rate of change of angular velocity during the drive. τnet: net axial torque (N·m); Total outside turning effect along the chosen axis. I, Ii, If: inertia, initially and finally (kg·m²); Resistance to changing spin; i/f label before/after the selected interval. ω, ωi, ωf: angular velocity, initially and finally (rad/s); Signed rate of turning. t: elapsed drive time (s); Duration of the constant torque. Krot: rotational kinetic energy (J); Energy of shared spinning motion. Laxis: axial angular momentum (kg·m²/s); Product Iω for this fixed-axis model. Unit key: m = metre, s = second, kg = kilogram, N = newton (kg·m/s²), J = joule (N·m), rad = radian (angle); MJ = one million joules. A dot joins multiplied units; / means per; ² means squared and ³ means cubed. Thus rad/s is radians per second and rad/s² is the change in rad/s each second.

example.title: An independent rotation example
steps: A rotor starts from rest with I=0.40 kg·m². Net torque 0.60 N·m acts for 2.0 s, giving α=1.5 rad/s² and ω=3.0 rad/s.
After removing that torque, its inertia changes to 0.20 kg·m². Conserve Laxis=0.40×3.0=1.2 kg·m²/s, giving final ω=6.0 rad/s.
Before rearrangement Krot=1.8 J; after it Krot=3.6 J. Internal work supplies the 1.8 J rise in this ideal endpoint account.

check.prompt: If a nonnegligible external axial torque persists during the rearrangement, what must be changed?
options: Include its angular impulse instead of setting Iiωi=Ifωf.
Ignore the torque because inertia is changing.
Set initial and final rotational energy equal regardless of internal work.
explanations: Angular momentum changes by the integrated external torque; the zero-torque equality no longer applies.
A changing inertia does not cancel external angular impulse.
An external torque does not justify omitting work or imposing kinetic-energy conservation.

apply.title: Try the idea in another case
apply.text: What limiting case should your torque-free rearrangement calculation pass if final inertia equals initial inertia?
apply.answer: The final angular velocity and endpoint rotational kinetic energy should equal their initial values, provided there is no residual internal motion or energy loss.

lessons.limits: This is a scalar fixed-axis idealization, not arbitrary tumbling or a human spinning demonstration. Explain missing energy transfers and external torques before applying it to a real system.

practice.prompt: A rotor initially at rest has I=0.75 kg·m². Constant net axial torque 1.5 N·m acts for 2.0 s. The torque is removed; then I falls to 0.50 kg·m² through an ideal internal rearrangement.

Angular momentum when the drive ends
Increase in endpoint rotational kinetic energy
parts.feedback: Initial rearrangement K=½×0.75×4²=6; final K=½×0.50×6²=9; rise 3.

practice.reasoning: Explain why the first interval adds angular momentum while the second conserves it, and where the 3 J energy rise comes from. Tight tolerances check the ideal arithmetic only.

equationGuide.meaning: During the drive, angular acceleration equals net torque divided by inertia. During torque-free rearrangement, initial inertia times initial angular velocity equals the final product. End-state spinning energy is half inertia times angular velocity squared.
